rows.statement: Explicitly declines to freeze an ADR declaring the Kernel boundary, citing the DDD review's list of items that must remain hypotheses (Proposition as fundamental primitive, Assertion as central aggregate, KnowledgeState as first-class object, a universal truth enum, a universal numeric knowledge vector, a complete question-operator taxonomy); instead proposes a 'KOS -- Kernel Boundary Discovery' artifact answering 'what minimum set of capabilities must be invariantly provided by KnowledgeOS regardless of domain, language, AI model, statistical method, or representation technology?', with a 20-row candidate classification table (e.g. Semantic identity/Concept/Evidence relation/Observation/Question: likely kernel; Proposition/Assertion: hypothesis; Truth: no universal truth engine, regime-dependent; Word/Sentence/Document/Embedding/LLM/ML model/Domain ontology/Knowledge graph: not kernel; Knowledge state: projection/hypothesis).

rows.anchor: What is the smallest thing KnowledgeOS must preserve so that knowledge can be expressed, questioned, challenged, evaluated, changed and reconstructed without losing its identity, context, provenance or epistemic meaning? That is the real Kernel question.
rows.statement: Poses the file's closing question, distinguished from 'how do we model knowledge?': 'what is the smallest thing KnowledgeOS must preserve so that knowledge can be expressed, questioned, challenged, evaluated, changed and reconstructed without losing its identity, context, provenance or epistemic meaning?', calling it the real Kernel question and stating that adding more classes, ML algorithms, topology, or Sanskrit grammar without answering it only makes the model larger, not more correct.

rows.anchor: The smallest thing KnowledgeOS must preserve is an identity-bearing, contextualized assertion record. ... This is a minimum preservation unit, not necessarily the fundamental aggregate or the definition of knowledge. ... PRESERVATION UNIT / CONSISTENCY BOUNDARY / PROJECTION VIEW ... These must not be collapsed.
rows.statement: Argues against freezing an 'AssertionAggregate' as the Kernel, distinguishing three concepts that must not be collapsed: a preservation unit (Assertion Record -- the identity-bearing, contextualized minimum unit KnowledgeOS must preserve, explicitly not necessarily the fundamental aggregate), a consistency boundary (Aggregate -- a transactional-consistency grouping), and a projection view (Knowledge State -- a derived read model); the identity-bearing-assertion-record claim is immediately qualified as a minimum preservation unit, not a definition of knowledge.
invariants: preservation unit ≠ consistency boundary ≠ projection view

rows.anchor: KnowledgeOS is infrastructure for preserving, relating, evaluating and reconstructing situated semantic commitments as knowledge changes over time. ... not "store knowledge" ... not "determine truth" ... preserve -> identify -> contextualize -> relate -> evaluate -> challenge -> change -> reconstruct.
rows.statement: Reformulates the KnowledgeOS mission as infrastructure for preserving/relating/evaluating/reconstructing situated semantic commitments as knowledge changes over time, explicitly not storing knowledge/documents, building a knowledge graph, determining truth, replacing human reasoning, or building AI memory, operationalized as an eight-step capability chain: preserve->identify->contextualize->relate->evaluate->challenge->change->reconstruct.

lineage_claims.target: KnowledgeOS = maintains semantic, epistemic and contextual integrity of a changing body of knowledge (S0509)
lineage_claims.quote: After everything we have explored, I would now formulate the KnowledgeOS mission as...

rows.anchor: stable identities; immutable historical records; typed relationships; explicit context; temporal distinctions; provenance chains; epistemic and lifecycle histories; contradiction and plurality; references across bounded contexts; reconstruction capability. ... our strongest candidate for the Kernel invariant surface.
rows.statement: Lists ten kernel principles (attributed to a referenced prior artifact) proposed as the strongest current candidate for the Kernel invariant surface: stable identities, immutable historical records, typed relationships, explicit context, temporal distinctions, provenance chains, epistemic and lifecycle histories, contradiction and plurality, cross-bounded-context references, and reconstruction capability.
dependencies: a referenced prior artifact (not individually identified in this file)

rows.anchor: what was said ... separately from what was observed ... separately from what was valid ... separately from what became effective ... separately from what was evaluated ... separately from what remains disputed. ... That generalizes beyond time. The same principle applies to the whole Kernel.
rows.statement: Generalizes a referenced temporal artifact's principle (different temporal roles must not collapse into one timestamp) into a Kernel-wide principle: what-was-said, what-was-observed, what-was-valid, what-became-effective, what-was-evaluated, and what-remains-disputed must all remain separately preserved, not just temporally but across every epistemic dimension.
invariants: distinct epistemic/temporal roles must not collapse into one representation

lineage_claims.quote: That generalizes beyond time. The same principle applies to the whole Kernel.

rows.anchor: Assertion should not become: Assertion, truth = TRUE. Instead: Assertion: semantic identity, context, temporal claims, provenance, authority, epistemic history, lifecycle, relationships {Evidence, Question, Assessment, Contradiction, Supersession}. And an assessment says: Assessment: subject, regime, context, evidence basis, evaluator, result, uncertainty, time.
rows.statement: Corrects a naive Assertion{truth=TRUE} model into Assertion{semantic identity, context, temporal claims, provenance, authority, epistemic history, lifecycle, relationships (Evidence/Question/Assessment/Contradiction/Supersession)} paired with a separate Assessment{subject, regime, context, evidence basis, evaluator, result, uncertainty, time}, so that evaluation is never encoded as mutating the assertion into an absolute truth.

rows.anchor: KnowledgeOS cannot guarantee: REALITY = TRUE. What it can guarantee is: "This assertion was evaluated as X under regime R, in context C, at time T, based on evidence E." That is not relativism. It is reconstructible epistemology.
rows.statement: Resolves the project's recurring 'truth' problem via a Reality->observation->Representation->semantic interpretation->Proposition->assertion->Assertion->assessment->Epistemic Assessment chain: KnowledgeOS cannot guarantee Reality=TRUE, only that 'this assertion was evaluated as X under regime R, in context C, at time T, based on evidence E' -- explicitly distinguished from relativism and named 'reconstructible epistemology'.

rows.anchor: "Topic" probably moves outside too ... "Kafka" can simultaneously belong to Distributed Systems, Messaging, Architecture, Infrastructure, Performance, Event Streaming, Security ... There isn't necessarily one canonical topic boundary. ... The topic is a way of looking at them.
rows.statement: Moves Topic outside the Kernel: 'Kafka' can simultaneously belong to seven different topical groupings (Distributed Systems, Messaging, Architecture, Infrastructure, Performance, Event Streaming, Security) with no canonical topic boundary, so the Knowledge Space generates different topic projections (e.g. Architecture/Security/Operations projections) over the same underlying assertions -- Topic is a projection/context construct, not a primitive Kernel object.

rows.anchor: The KnowledgeOS Kernel boundary ends where KnowledgeOS can no longer make a domain-independent structural guarantee about the identity, context, provenance, temporal meaning, epistemic history, relationships, or reconstructibility of a knowledge-bearing assertion. ... Kernel test: If this capability is removed, can KnowledgeOS still preserve and reconstruct the identity and epistemic history of a situated semantic commitment?
rows.statement: Proposes a falsifiable Kernel-boundary criterion and test: the Kernel ends where KnowledgeOS can no longer make a domain-independent structural guarantee about identity/context/provenance/temporal-meaning/epistemic-history/relationships/reconstructibility; the test for any candidate capability is 'if this capability is removed, can KnowledgeOS still preserve and reconstruct the identity and epistemic history of a situated semantic commitment?' -- yes means outside the Kernel, no means a candidate Kernel concern.

rows.anchor: Stable identity: Yes ... Question structure: Needs boundary test ... Answer generation: Outside ... Truth determination: Outside/regime ... Topics: Probably projection ... Vector DB: Outside.
rows.statement: Applies the Kernel test to 24 candidates: yes-inside (stable identity, semantic identity/reference, context, temporal semantics [policy-driven], provenance, assertion history, epistemic history, lifecycle history, typed relationships, contradiction representation [likely]); needs-test (question structure, topics [probably projection]); outside (answer generation, truth determination, statistical inference, LLM, embedding, documents, words, sentences, domain ontology, UI, search, vector DB).

rows.anchor: KnowledgeOS Kernel = the domain-independent infrastructure that preserves the identity, context, provenance, temporal semantics, epistemic history and relationships necessary to reconstruct situated semantic commitments over time. ... evaluation itself may not belong entirely inside the Kernel.
rows.statement: Refines the Kernel definition from S0509's 'what makes a knowledge system capable of distinguishing, relating, evaluating and evolving claims' into 'the domain-independent infrastructure that preserves the identity, context, provenance, temporal semantics, epistemic history and relationships necessary to reconstruct situated semantic commitments over time', explicitly removing 'evaluating' from the Kernel's own responsibility since an Assertion Aggregate should not decide universal truth, objective evidence sufficiency, or universal relevance -- the Kernel provides assessment infrastructure, not the universal evaluator.
dependencies: Knowledge Kernel = what makes a knowledge system capable of distinguishing, relating, evaluating and evolving claims (S0509)

lineage_claims.target: Knowledge Kernel = what makes a knowledge system capable of distinguishing, relating, evaluating and evolving claims (S0509)
lineage_claims.quote: One thing I would change in the previous formulation ... I would now make it more precise

rows.anchor: Can we quantify knowledge? ... Not directly. Instead we quantify properties of the knowledge state. ... assertion coverage, evidence coverage, contradiction density, temporal stability, provenance completeness, semantic ambiguity, uncertainty, question coverage, answer completeness, boundary stability ... more defensible than inventing a single Knowledge Score.

unknown_candidate.why_uncertain: Another candidate list of measurable knowledge-projection properties, in the same family as the many cumulative knowledge-state tuples proposed earlier in this batch, but explicitly reframed as properties of a projection rather than of 'knowledge' itself.

rows.statement: Rejects direct quantification of 'knowledge', instead proposing quantification of ten measurable properties of a Knowledge Projection (assertion coverage, evidence coverage, contradiction density, temporal stability, provenance completeness, semantic ambiguity, uncertainty, question coverage, answer completeness, boundary stability), on which statistical methods can operate -- operationalizing the project's 'inverse statistical' idea and stated to be more scientifically defensible than inventing a single Knowledge Score.

rows.anchor: Topology should not try to define what knowledge is. Instead it can investigate: connected components, clusters, gaps, boundaries, bridges, isolated assertions, contradiction regions, unstable regions. ... Same for Dhātu, Karaka, Pramāṇa, ML, statistical inference, graph analysis. They become lenses over KnowledgeOS, not competing definitions of the Kernel.
rows.statement: Reframes topology (and by extension Dhatu, Karaka, Pramana, ML, statistical inference, graph analysis) as external analytical lenses operating over the Kernel's preserved relational structure -- investigating connected components/clusters/gaps/boundaries/bridges/isolated assertions/contradiction regions/unstable regions -- rather than as competing definitions of what the Kernel or knowledge itself is, called a very important simplification.

rows.anchor: Is "assertion" really the universal center? Consider: a constitutional rule; an observed fact; a scientific hypothesis; a definition; a mathematical theorem; a question; a model prediction; a design decision; a requirement; a historical event. Are all of these best represented as assertions? Maybe. But we should prove that, rather than assume it.
rows.statement: Poses an unresolved foundational question: is Assertion really the universal semantic/epistemic center, tested against ten candidate knowledge-bearing types (constitutional rule, observed fact, scientific hypothesis, definition, mathematical theorem, question, model prediction, design decision, requirement, historical event), explicitly warning the claim must be proven rather than assumed.
dependencies: AssertionRecord as candidate preservation unit (same file)

rows.anchor: KOS Kernel Boundary & Primitive Discovery ... Assume the current Assertion-centered model is wrong. Try to break it. ... Observation, Definition, Rule, Requirement, Hypothesis, Fact claim, Inference, Prediction, Question, Answer, Decision, Constitutional principle, Mathematical proposition, Historical statement, Contradictory assertions, Temporal assertions, Unknown knowledge, Knowledge gaps. ... If no, we have discovered the boundary or a missing primitive.
rows.statement: Proposes the next research exercise, 'KOS Kernel Boundary & Primitive Discovery', deliberately adversarial: assume the Assertion-centered model is wrong and try to break it against eighteen candidate types (Observation, Definition, Rule, Requirement, Hypothesis, Fact claim, Inference, Prediction, Question, Answer, Decision, Constitutional principle, Mathematical proposition, Historical statement, Contradictory assertions, Temporal assertions, Unknown knowledge, Knowledge gaps), asking for each whether the candidate Kernel can preserve it without inventing special cases -- a 'no' result discovers either the boundary or a missing primitive, described as the point where the lens series becomes a rigorous architecture-discovery method rather than a collection of modelling ideas.

rows.anchor: Is Assertion itself fundamental, or is it merely a useful abstraction over more primitive relationships? ... Agent -asserts-> Proposition -applies-in-> Context ... Assertion is the relationship/event that binds these together.
rows.statement: Applies the eliminativism test to Assertion (currently modeled as owning Proposition/Context/Agent/Time/Provenance/Epistemic history), asking whether Assertion is fundamental or merely the relationship/event binding a more primitive Agent-asserts->Proposition-applies-in->Context structure -- an object-centric KnowledgeAssertionRecord versus a relationship/event-centric Assertion Act (by Agent, at Time, in Context, under Authority, with Provenance) -- stating KnowledgeOS may ultimately need the event-centric formulation.

rows.anchor: What entities and relationships must exist in the KnowledgeOS Kernel such that every useful higher-level knowledge construct can be reconstructed without loss? ... Is Assertion genuinely a non-redundant KnowledgeOS primitive, or is it itself a useful higher-level object emerging from more fundamental assertion-events, propositions, contexts, agents and relations? I would not freeze the Assertion Aggregate until we answer that question.
rows.statement: Sharpens the Kernel question from 'what is the smallest thing KnowledgeOS must preserve?' (answered: an identity-bearing assertion relationship, S0510) to 'what entities and relationships must exist in the Kernel such that every useful higher-level knowledge construct can be reconstructed without loss?', summarizing Merricks' method as a seven-step discipline (start with ordinary conceptual objects -> ask what underlying structure makes them useful -> remove the candidate -> see what capabilities disappear -> nothing essential disappears = projection/abstraction -> non-redundant work disappears = candidate primitive -> preserve the underlying structure even when eliminating the higher-level object), and explicitly declines to freeze the Assertion Aggregate until the open question (is Assertion genuinely non-redundant?) is answered.

lineage_claims.target: "what is the smallest thing KnowledgeOS must preserve?" (S0510)
lineage_claims.quote: Now I would sharpen the question to...

rows.anchor: What is the minimal formal structure required for a system to represent, relate, evaluate, preserve, and reason about knowledge claims without confusing representation, truth, evidence, meaning, time, modality, and epistemic status? ... stop trying to answer: "What is the one fundamental object called Knowledge?" and instead investigate: "What are the irreducible distinctions that KnowledgeOS must preserve?"
rows.statement: Reframes the research problem after incorporating Merricks: not 'building a database of facts', but determining the minimal formal structure required to represent/relate/evaluate/preserve/reason about knowledge claims without confusing representation/truth/evidence/meaning/time/modality/epistemic-status; replaces 'what is the one fundamental object called Knowledge?' with 'what are the irreducible distinctions that KnowledgeOS must preserve?' as the guiding question.

rows.anchor: Merricks: Truth cannot be reduced to truthmaking/evidence/aboutness. O'Connor: Persons, objects, properties, powers, causes, reasons, intentions and actions cannot simply be collapsed into events or objects. Our KnowledgeOS investigation: Knowledge must remain reconstructible, contextual, governed and evidentially traceable. ... Is this a primitive entity, a relation, a property, a state, a representation, a perspective, or merely a useful projection?
rows.statement: States three converging constraints from Merricks, O'Connor, and the project's own KnowledgeOS investigation, concluding the right next step is not to declare an ontology but to run a 'Knowledge Space Ontological Discovery' over 22 candidates (Persons, Objects, Properties, Events, States, Actions, Agents, Causes, Effects, Powers, Capacities, Reasons, Intentions, Claims, Propositions, Truth, Evidence, Sources, Contexts, Time, Modality, Explanation), asking of each whether it is a primitive entity, relation, property, state, representation, perspective, or merely a useful projection.

rows.anchor: You have spent 130 documents demonstrating that "what is knowledge?" is not answerable. The decidable engineering question is: What is the minimal record such that any of these epistemic regimes could later be run over it? ... Fagin's model is about inference; your 113243 position is about preservation. Different obligations, different invariants.
rows.statement: Reframes the central research question after ~130 documents of unanswered 'what is knowledge?' inquiry into a decidable engineering question: 'what is the minimal record such that any of these epistemic regimes could later be run over it?', converting an unanswerable ontological question into a testable preservation question, and explaining an asymmetry the reviewed document missed -- Fagin's model addresses inference, while the S0510 ('113243') position addresses preservation; these are different obligations with different invariants.
invariants: inference obligations and preservation obligations require different invariants

rows.anchor: a boundary that supports every semantics protects no invariant. In DDD terms a consistency boundary exists to protect an invariant atomically; if every semantics is pluggable, the invariants live in the plugins and the Kernel degrades to a generic store. ... What does the Kernel decide that no regime may override?
rows.statement: Sharpens F-4: 'the Kernel supports multiple epistemic regimes without imposing one semantics' is correct as anti-overreach but dangerous as architecture unqualified, since a boundary supporting every semantics protects no invariant (in DDD terms, a consistency boundary exists to protect an invariant atomically; if every semantics is pluggable, invariants live in the plugins and the Kernel degrades to a generic store); poses the unanswered question 'what does the Kernel decide that no regime may override?', noting the corpus's minimum-preservation-unit position (S0510) is a more decidable answer than possible worlds, which S0523 fails to cite.
missing: a direct answer to 'what does the Kernel decide that no regime may override?'
dependencies: Kernel should support multiple epistemic regimes (S0523)

rows.anchor: Preservation and inference are different obligations with different invariants. The Kernel is a preservation boundary. Possible-worlds semantics, pramāṇa, statistical inference and algorithmic knowledge are all regimes that read the record. That framing satisfies §28 while giving F-4 a real answer: the Kernel's non-negotiable job is to keep the record sufficient and un-foreclosing, not to adjudicate truth.
rows.statement: Answers the F-4 open question directly: the Kernel's non-negotiable job is to keep the record sufficient and un-foreclosing, not to adjudicate truth; possible-worlds semantics, the Pramana regime, statistical inference, and algorithmic knowledge are all 'regimes that read the record' rather than parts of the Kernel itself, since preservation (what must be recorded so a model can be applied later) and inference (computing what is known given a model) are different obligations with different invariants.
invariants: preservation and inference are different obligations with different invariants

rows.anchor: OQ-1 What does the Kernel decide that no regime may override? (F-4 — unanswered) ... OQ-3 Can unawareness be represented in the record at all, or only its effects? (F-2) ... OQ-5 Does the corpus's established minimum preservation unit already subsume §27's tuple — making the tuple a regime schema rather than a Kernel model?
rows.statement: Closes with five explicit open questions left unresolved by the review: (OQ-1) what does the Kernel decide that no regime may override; (OQ-2) is the Kernel a preservation boundary only, or does it also own any inference; (OQ-3) can unawareness be represented in the record at all, or only its effects; (OQ-4) which of the three 'Knowledge Space' senses, if any, is the one the Kernel bounds; (OQ-5) does the corpus's established minimum preservation unit already subsume the K-tuple, making the tuple a regime schema rather than a Kernel model.
missing: answers to all five open questions
dependencies: three senses of Knowledge Space (S0524, S0525)

rows.anchor: What is the minimal record such that any epistemic regime could later be run over it? I think this is the most important sentence in the whole critique. ... Different epistemic regimes -> same preserved substrate -> Fagin, Bayesian, Pramāṇa -> assessments.
rows.statement: Fully adopts the critique's reframe ('what is the minimal record such that any epistemic regime could later be run over it?') as the single most important sentence of the review, since KnowledgeOS need not settle philosophy before preserving what multiple philosophies/models require, formalized as: different epistemic regimes (Fagin, Bayesian, Pramana) operate over the same preserved substrate to produce assessments.

rows.anchor: Preserve: identity, source, representation, semantic reference, context, scope, time, observation, assertion, provenance, relationships, change, conflict, authority, assessment history, question/answer history. Outside: Fagin epistemic logic, Bayesian model, Pramāṇa regime, statistical inference, LLM, topology, graph algorithms, causal model, human review. The Kernel should retain enough information that these regimes can be applied later without destroying the historical substrate.
rows.statement: Introduces the 'preservation substrate' concept as the clearest synthesis reached: the Kernel preserves sixteen named items (identity, source, representation, semantic reference, context, scope, time, observation, assertion, provenance, relationships, change, conflict, authority, assessment history, question/answer history), while reasoning over that substrate (Fagin epistemic logic, Bayesian models, Pramana regime, statistical inference, LLM, topology, graph algorithms, causal models, human review) stays entirely outside the Kernel, whose concrete responsibility is to retain enough information that these regimes can be applied later without destroying the historical substrate.

rows.anchor: The Kernel boundary is the minimum preservation boundary required to reconstruct, under more than one epistemic regime, the identity, context, provenance, temporal state, relationships and history of a knowledge-bearing episode. Anything whose absence makes such reconstruction impossible is a Kernel candidate. Anything that merely determines how to reason over the preserved data belongs outside the Kernel.
rows.statement: States the sharpest Kernel-boundary definition reached in the batch: the Kernel boundary is the minimum preservation boundary required to reconstruct, under more than one epistemic regime, the identity/context/provenance/temporal-state/relationships/history of a knowledge-bearing episode; anything whose absence makes such reconstruction impossible is a Kernel candidate, anything that merely determines how to reason over the preserved data belongs outside -- explicitly sharper than 'Kernel contains concepts like truth, proposition, knowledge.'

lineage_claims.target: Kernel test (S0510) and Kernel boundary formulations across S0509-S0525
lineage_claims.quote: This also gives us a better definition of the Kernel boundary.

rows.anchor: We are not trying to discover the one universal definition of knowledge. We are trying to discover the minimum historical and semantic preservation substrate that allows different legitimate epistemic regimes to reconstruct, evaluate, challenge and evolve knowledge without losing identity, context, provenance, temporal meaning, or accountability. ... This is where I would stop the ontology expansion.
rows.statement: States the final rewritten research position closing the whole McGinn-Floridi-Dretske-Fagin arc: the goal is not the one universal definition of knowledge but the minimum historical and semantic preservation substrate allowing legitimate epistemic regimes to reconstruct/evaluate/challenge/evolve knowledge without losing identity, context, provenance, temporal meaning, or accountability, with a final architecture split into Preservation Substrate (identity, provenance, context, scope, time, observations, assertions, relationships, history, conflicts, authority, assessment history) versus Reasoning Regimes (Fagin, Bayesian, Pramana, ML/Statistics, LLM); explicitly declares this the point to stop ontology expansion.

rows.anchor: KNOWLEDGEOS PRESERVATION KERNEL: Identity, Context/scope, Temporal position, Representation provenance, Observation/source reference, Assertion/proposition reference, Relationships, Agent/epistemic participant, Authority/accountability reference, Change history, Conflict history, Assessment history, Question/inquiry history. ... deliberately removed: Truth engine, Possible-world engine, Bayesian engine, Knowledge score, Universal epistemology, LLM, Topic hierarchy.
rows.statement: Reduces the candidate Kernel, after four books plus the critique cycle, to thirteen items (Identity, Context/scope, Temporal position, Representation provenance, Observation/source reference, Assertion/proposition reference, Relationships, Agent/epistemic participant, Authority/accountability reference, Change history, Conflict history, Assessment history, Question/inquiry history), explicitly excluding a Truth engine, Possible-world engine, Bayesian engine, Knowledge score, Universal epistemology, LLM, and Topic hierarchy as belonging outside.

lineage_claims.quote: After the four books + Claude's critique, I would reduce our candidate Kernel to something much smaller

rows.anchor: Something is represented. Something is observed. Something is asserted. Something is related to something else. Someone/something participates. Something happens at some time. Something changes. An assertion may support or conflict with another. A question may be asked. An assessment may be made. A history must remain reconstructible. That is probably closer to the actual Kernel than any philosophical ontology we have constructed so far.
rows.statement: Applies the Zero Lens by removing every named source (McGinn, Floridi, Dretske, Fagin, Sanskrit lenses, statistical models, possible worlds, LLMs, knowledge graphs, DDD terminology), leaving a ten-statement residual (something is represented/observed/asserted/related-to-something-else; someone/something participates; something happens at a time; something changes; an assertion may support or conflict with another; a question may be asked; an assessment may be made; a history must remain reconstructible), judged closer to the actual Kernel than any philosophical ontology constructed so far.

rows.anchor: PRESERVATION SUBSTRATE: Identity, Agent/epistemic participant, Context, Time, Epistemic input, Input provenance, Assertion/proposition reference, Epistemic attitude/assessment, State-transition event, Previous state reference, Resulting-state reference, Change type, Rationale/commitment reference, Conflict/incompatibility, Evidence/source, Entrenchment assessment. Notice what is not here: possible worlds, Bayesian probabilities, logic engine, truth engine, LLM, topic hierarchy, embedding.
rows.statement: Revises the candidate Preservation Substrate to sixteen items (Identity, Agent/epistemic participant, Context, Time, Epistemic input, Input provenance, Assertion/proposition reference, Epistemic attitude/assessment, State-transition event, Previous state reference, Resulting-state reference, Change type, Rationale/commitment reference, Conflict/incompatibility, Evidence/source, Entrenchment assessment), explicitly excluding possible worlds, Bayesian probabilities, logic engine, truth engine, LLM, topic hierarchy, and embedding as belonging to external regimes.

lineage_claims.quote: This book makes me revise our previous candidate.

rows.anchor: Inside the Kernel: WHO, WHAT, WHEN, FROM WHAT INPUT, UNDER WHICH CONTEXT, WITH WHAT EPISTEMIC ATTITUDE, WHAT CHANGED, WHY IT CHANGED, WHAT WAS RETAINED, WHAT WAS RETRACTED, WHAT HISTORY LED HERE. Outside the Kernel: How should we revise? How should we calculate probability? ... How should we summarize? That separation is becoming remarkably clean.
rows.statement: States the cleanest Inside/Outside Kernel split reached in the batch: inside are the facts needed to reconstruct who/what/when/from-what-input/under-which-context/with-what-attitude/what-changed/why/what-was-retained/what-was-retracted/what-history-led-here; outside are the rules answering how to revise, calculate probability, rank possibilities, infer causality, explain, reason, parse language, or summarize.

rows.anchor: Infinite Knowledge Space exists independently of our limited ability to perceive, represent, reason about, and store it. ... How do we capture a faithful state of that projection at time (t), without pretending that we captured the whole infinite Knowledge Space? ... we need a snapshot of the epistemic projection, not a snapshot of Knowledge itself.
rows.statement: States the file's central architectural problem: an infinite Knowledge Space exists independently of any agent's limited perceiving/representing/reasoning/storing capacity; the precise engineering question is how to capture a faithful state of the accessible projection at time t without pretending to have captured the whole infinite space; the answer is a snapshot of the epistemic projection, not of Knowledge itself.

rows.anchor: S_t ≠ Ω. Sₜ is not the Knowledge Space. It is: what the system can currently represent, distinguish, justify, and use about the Knowledge Space under a specified regime and boundary at time (t). ... two systems may contain exactly the same facts but have different epistemic states. System A: knows why X happened, has evidence, considers alternative Y unlikely. System B: knows X happened, has no causal explanation, is uncertain about Y.
rows.statement: Formalizes S_t != Omega: the captured state is what the system can currently represent/distinguish/justify/use about the Knowledge Space under a specified regime and boundary at time t; demonstrates via a worked example that two systems sharing identical fact sets can have different epistemic states (one has a causal explanation and considers an alternative unlikely, the other lacks explanation and remains uncertain), so a snapshot must capture the epistemic system's state, not merely its stored propositions.

rows.anchor: S_t = (B_t, E_t, Q_t, C_t, T_t, R_t, A_t, U_t, X_t) ... current accepted/held propositions, evidence/provenance, unresolved questions, context and boundary, temporal scope, epistemic regime, awareness/accessibility, uncertainty/plausibility, contradictions/conflicts. This is not yet a final schema.

unknown_candidate.why_uncertain: Another cumulative knowledge-state tuple in the same growing family across the batch, explicitly disclaimed as not-yet-final.

rows.statement: Proposes a nine-component snapshot state vector S_t=(B_t,E_t,Q_t,C_t,T_t,R_t,A_t,U_t,X_t) (held propositions, evidence/provenance, unresolved questions, context/boundary, temporal scope, epistemic regime, awareness/accessibility, uncertainty/plausibility, contradictions/conflicts), explicitly not a final schema but the conceptual shape of the snapshot.

rows.anchor: capturedAt, validAt, observedAt, assertedAt, evaluatedAt, effectiveAt ... "What did we know at 13:47?" is different from "What was true at 13:47?" and different again from "What did we learn at 13:47 about something that happened at 11:00?"
rows.statement: Reinforces that a snapshot's time must not be a single timestamp, distinguishing six temporal roles (capturedAt, validAt, observedAt, assertedAt, evaluatedAt, effectiveAt), illustrated by 'what did we know at 13:47?' differing from 'what was true at 13:47?' differing again from 'what did we learn at 13:47 about something that happened at 11:00?'

rows.anchor: Snapshot Sₜ answers: What was the epistemic state at time (t)? History H[0...t] answers: How did the system arrive at that state? ... Two systems could have the same Sₜ but different histories ... for assurance, replay, audit, and governance, that difference may matter.
rows.statement: Distinguishes Snapshot (S_t, what the epistemic state was at time t) from History (H[0..t], how the system arrived there); two systems can share identical S_t while differing in H, a difference that matters for assurance, replay, audit, and governance -- so KnowledgeOS should preserve STATE plus TRANSITION HISTORY together, not either alone.

rows.anchor: A Knowledge State (S_t) is a time-indexed, context-bounded, regime-relative projection of the infinite Knowledge Space containing the semantic commitments, available evidence, unresolved questions, epistemic attitudes, relevant relations, and known limitations accessible to a specified participant or system at time (t). ... It is deliberately not: "the truth at time (t)."
rows.statement: States a working definition of Knowledge State: a time-indexed, context-bounded, regime-relative projection of the infinite Knowledge Space, containing semantic commitments, available evidence, unresolved questions, epistemic attitudes, relevant relations, and known limitations accessible to a specified participant/system at time t -- deliberately not 'the truth at time t'.
invariants: Knowledge State ≠ the truth at time t

rows.anchor: Projection P: source-space = Ω, boundary = B, level-of-abstraction = L, purpose = U, epistemic-regime = R, participant = A, time = t. Then: S_t = P(Ω | B,L,U,R,A,t). This is a very useful conceptual equation.
rows.statement: Formalizes an explicit Projection object (source-space Omega, boundary B, level-of-abstraction L, purpose U, epistemic-regime R, participant A, time t) and the conceptual equation S_t = P(Omega | B,L,U,R,A,t): the state is produced by applying a projection function to the infinite space under explicit, recorded conditions -- described as implementable and reasonable-about, unlike the raw infinite space.
missing: definition of the projection function P

rows.anchor: Suppose proposition P isn't in the snapshot. That does not automatically mean: P = unknown. It could mean: outside boundary, not observed, not represented, not accessible, not asked, not evaluated, not relevant, unknown. ... Coverage state: represented, observed, assessed, unresolved, excluded by boundary, not yet encountered.
rows.statement: Distinguishes 'missing from the snapshot' from 'unknown': an absent proposition may instead be outside-boundary, not-observed, not-represented, not-accessible, not-asked, not-evaluated, or not-relevant; proposes a six-state 'epistemic coverage' classification per question/concept (represented, observed, assessed, unresolved, excluded by boundary, not yet encountered), called critical for quantification.

rows.anchor: Coverage: C_t = relevant epistemic scope represented / declared scope. Uncertainty: U_t = H(P_t). Conflict: X_t = unresolved contradictory commitments / relevant commitments. Provenance coverage: P_t = claims with reconstructible provenance / claims in projection. Question resolution: Q_t = resolved obligations / active obligations. These are dimensions of the state. Not the state itself.
rows.statement: Proposes five measurable ratio dimensions of a Knowledge State, replacing a single Knowledge=0.8 score: Coverage (relevant scope represented / declared scope), Uncertainty (entropy of the current probability/plausibility distribution), Conflict (unresolved contradictory commitments / relevant commitments), Provenance coverage (claims with reconstructible provenance / claims in projection), Question resolution (resolved obligations / active obligations) -- explicitly dimensions of the state, not the state itself.

rows.anchor: We don't actually need to capture the entire infinite history. ... immutable events + deterministic projection + snapshot/checkpoint ... This gives us both: replayability and efficient current-state access without pretending to store infinity.
rows.statement: Resolves the 'infinite time' concern: KnowledgeOS need not capture the entire infinite history, only a finite certificate of how the current state was obtained (H_0:t -> S(t)), implemented as immutable events + deterministic projection rule + snapshot/checkpoint, giving both replayability and efficient current-state access without storing infinity.

rows.anchor: State Reconstruction Invariant. For every Knowledge State (S_t): S_t = Project(H_{≤t}, B, L, U, R, A) or, if the projection is not deterministic: S_t = Project(H_{≤t}, B, L, U, R, A; θ) where the regime parameters θ are themselves recorded.
rows.statement: Names the 'State Reconstruction Invariant', formalizing the Kernel's responsibility as making every Knowledge State S_t reconstructible as Project(H≤t, B, L, U, R, A), or Project(H≤t, B, L, U, R, A; theta) if the projection is non-deterministic, with the regime parameters theta themselves recorded -- the Kernel need not know 'all knowledge', only make captured states reconstructible from preserved history under declared conditions.

rows.anchor: there isn't one universal KnowledgeState. There can be: S_t^A, S_t^B, S_t^G, ... all derived from the same underlying preserved substrate but under different perspectives.
rows.statement: States there is no single universal KnowledgeState: distinct per-participant/organization states S_t^A, S_t^B, S_t^G are all derived from the same preserved substrate (identity/provenance/time/context/boundary/observations/commitments/transitions/regime references) via projection, but reflect different perspectives -- a strong consequence of the projection/regime model.
invariants: no single universal KnowledgeState exists; only per-participant/organization projections

rows.anchor: "goes back into the Knowledge Space" should not mean that the agent changes some universal cosmic database. It means: the agent's newly produced representations, observations, arguments, and commitments become new structures that can themselves become objects of future inquiry.
rows.statement: Refines the intuition that knowledge 'goes back into the Knowledge Space' after being processed: this does not mean the agent modifies a universal cosmic database, but that the agent's newly produced representations/observations/arguments/commitments become new structures that can themselves later become objects of future inquiry -- a safer architectural interpretation.

rows.anchor: P: "The service is slow." Then Q: "The team believes that the service is slow." Then R: "The architecture board has verified that the team believes the service is slow." Then S: "The verification process itself is reliable." ... This is one reason the space can be effectively unbounded.
rows.statement: Illustrates the recursive knowledge-about-knowledge property with a four-step regress (claim about the service -> belief that the team holds the claim -> verification that the team holds the belief -> reliability of the verification process itself), naming this one reason the Knowledge Space is effectively unbounded.

rows.anchor: S_t^A ≠ S_t^B ≠ S_t^G without concluding Reality_A ≠ Reality_B ≠ Reality_G. ... Each state is a projection. Different observations, capacities, boundaries, purposes, abstractions, evidence, reasoning regimes produce different states. That is perfectly compatible with there being one underlying Knowledge Space.
rows.statement: States the central refinement: different participants' knowledge states can legitimately diverge (S_t^A != S_t^B != S_t^G) without implying divergent underlying reality, since different observations/capacities/boundaries/purposes/abstractions/evidence/reasoning-regimes each produce different projections of one shared Knowledge Space.
invariants: divergent projections do not imply divergent reality

rows.anchor: I would not impose: Different projections must never contain contradictory propositions. That is too strong. ... Different knowledge projections must not be required to agree syntactically; they must remain semantically reconcilable within the larger Knowledge Space when their contexts, times, boundaries and epistemic regimes are taken into account.
rows.statement: Rejects 'different projections must never contain contradictory propositions' as too strong, replacing it with 'projections need not agree syntactically but must remain semantically reconcilable given their contexts/times/boundaries/regimes', illustrated by an apparently contradictory pair ('the service is healthy' vs 'the service is unhealthy') that resolves once differing observation times, architectural layers, or instance-vs-global scope are accounted for.
invariants: projections must be semantically reconcilable, not syntactically identical

lineage_claims.target: 'different projections must never contain contradictory propositions' (rejected candidate principle, same file)
lineage_claims.quote: I would not impose ... That is too strong.

rows.anchor: Every local knowledge projection should be oriented toward the structure it is attempting to represent, rather than becoming a self-contained absolute reality. ... epistemic orientation. O(S_t) = (scope, purpose, LoA, regime, time). ... two states can be compared correctly ... by first comparing O(S_t^A) and O(S_t^B).
rows.statement: States a candidate foundational principle -- every local knowledge projection should be oriented toward the structure it represents rather than becoming a self-contained absolute reality -- introducing 'epistemic orientation' O(S_t)=(scope, purpose, LoA, regime, time) as what a state is trying to describe, from which perspective, for what purpose, under which constraints; two states should be compared via their orientations O(S_t^A) vs O(S_t^B) before comparing their content.

rows.anchor: Infinite Knowledge Space Ω ... Knowledge Projection P_i(Ω) ... Knowledge State S_t^i ... Knowledge History H_{≤t}^i ... S_t^i = P_i(Ω, H_{≤t}^i). This is a much more precise formulation.
rows.statement: Refines the projection hierarchy into four explicit levels -- Omega (unbounded space of possible objects/states/relations/facts/ideas/explanations), Knowledge Projection P_i(Omega) (a bounded view produced by a person/agent/system/organization/inquiry), Knowledge State S_t^i (that projection's state at a time), Knowledge History H≤t^i (how it evolved) -- combined as S_t^i = P_i(Omega, H≤t^i).

lineage_claims.quote: This is a much more precise formulation of what you have been describing.

rows.anchor: Projection Compatibility Principle. Knowledge projections need not be identical, but their differences must be interpretable through their declared context, boundary, time, purpose, abstraction level, evidence, and epistemic regime. ... same referent? same time? same scope? same Level of Abstraction? same proposition? same regime? ... true contradiction, complementary perspectives, temporal change, scope difference, abstraction difference, epistemic incompleteness.
rows.statement: Names the 'Projection Compatibility Principle': projections need not be identical but their differences must be interpretable through declared context/boundary/time/purpose/abstraction/evidence/regime; when two projections appear to disagree, the Kernel tests same-referent/same-time/same-scope/same-LoA/same-proposition/same-regime before classifying the disagreement as true contradiction, complementary perspectives, temporal change, scope difference, abstraction difference, or epistemic incompleteness.

rows.anchor: Local epistemic consistency: Does this projection internally hang together? ... Cross-projection compatibility: Can these different projections coexist? ... Truth orientation: Are the projections making claims intended to correspond to the underlying domain? ... Reality adequacy: How well does the projection survive independent observation/verification?
rows.statement: Distinguishes four separate questions previously conflated under 'truth': Local epistemic consistency (does a projection internally hang together), Cross-projection compatibility (can different projections coexist), Truth orientation (are claims intended to correspond to the domain), and Reality adequacy (how well the projection survives independent verification) -- one projection can be internally consistent but incomplete, while another is more complete but weaker evidenced.
dependencies: Truth != correspondence-as-reduction / robust truth property (S0513, S0519)

rows.anchor: Knowledge doesn't necessarily move: false → true. It can move: coarse, refined, expanded, qualified, corrected, recontextualized. ... S1: The system is slow. S2: The API is slow. S3: The API latency is high only under load. S4: caused by database contention. S5: triggered by query pattern X. The later states do not merely replace the earlier one. They orient more deeply into the Knowledge Space.
rows.statement: Reframes knowledge evolution away from a false->true movement toward a coarse->refined->expanded->qualified->corrected->recontextualized progression, illustrated by a five-stage worked example (system slow -> API slow -> latency high only under load -> caused by database contention -> triggered by a specific query pattern), where later states do not merely replace earlier ones but orient more deeply into the Knowledge Space, matching the project's 'going deeper and deeper' intuition.
dependencies: infinite knowledge depth intuition (S0507, S0513, S0521)

rows.anchor: Knowledge progress could mean: A projection becomes more informative or structurally adequate relative to a defined inquiry and boundary. ... Progress = (ΔC,ΔU,ΔE,ΔX,ΔD,ΔQ) ... far more meaningful than: Knowledge_new > Knowledge_old as one number.
rows.statement: Defines Knowledge Progress as a projection becoming more informative or structurally adequate relative to a defined inquiry and boundary, formalized as a six-dimension delta vector Progress=(delta-Coverage, delta-Uncertainty, delta-Evidence-quality, delta-Contradiction-reduction, delta-Explanatory-depth, delta-Question-resolution), explicitly more meaningful than a scalar Knowledge_new > Knowledge_old comparison.

rows.anchor: Knowledge exists as local, time-dependent projections of an unbounded Knowledge Space. ... These projections need not be identical, but they should remain semantically reconcilable and oriented toward the same underlying Knowledge Space rather than treating their local projection as the whole of reality. ... KnowledgeOS does not own the Knowledge Space. It preserves and relates the projections, transitions, evidence, boundaries, and orientations through which participants engage with it.
rows.statement: States the file's deepest formulation, called one of the strongest conceptual formulations reached so far: knowledge exists as local, time-dependent projections of an unbounded Knowledge Space, legitimately differing across participants due to differing observations/capacities/boundaries/purposes/regimes, but remaining semantically reconcilable and oriented toward the same underlying space rather than each being treated as the whole of reality; correspondingly, KnowledgeOS does not own the Knowledge Space -- it preserves and relates the projections, transitions, evidence, boundaries, and orientations through which participants engage with it.

rows.anchor: the Kernel may need an explicit primitive for Orientation / Perspective, or we may discover that orientation is derivable from participant + purpose + boundary + Level of Abstraction + epistemic regime. That is exactly the kind of question the Zero Lens should test next.
rows.statement: Leaves open whether the Kernel needs an explicit Orientation/Perspective primitive, or whether orientation is fully derivable from participant+purpose+boundary+Level-of-Abstraction+epistemic-regime, naming it the next question the Zero Lens/eliminativism test should address.

rows.anchor: Not all projections are projections of the same kind of reality. Some project natural facts; some project semantic structures; some project institutional statuses; some project epistemic states.
rows.statement: Refines the per-agent projection model (from S0529/S0530) by arguing not all projections project the same kind of reality -- some project natural facts, some semantic structures, some institutional statuses, some epistemic states -- and that KnowledgeOS must preserve which kind of projection a given projection is, calling this a major boundary condition.

rows.anchor:
McGinn
  │
  └── Identity / Existence / Predication / Truth / Modality
rows.statement: Synthesizes the whole six-book research arc into one table (McGinn: Identity/Existence/Predication/Truth/Modality; Floridi: Levels of Abstraction/Observables/Relevance; Dretske: Information/Transmission/Possibility reduction; Fagin: Agents/Epistemic states/Shared knowledge; Gardenfors: Expansion/Revision/Contraction/Entrenchment; Searle: Social reality/Status/Institutions/Collective intentionality/Deontic powers) and a boxed chain: Infinite Knowledge Space -> Reality/Semantics/Institutions -> Observations -> Epistemic States -> Projections.

rows.anchor: knowledge = capacity to write information
rows.statement: Rejects the proposed formulation 'knowledge = capacity to write information' as too narrow, on the grounds that a person can know something without being able to write it down, and an institutional system can preserve information without 'knowing' it in the epistemic sense.

rows.anchor: So **capacity** sits between the infinite space and the particular knowledge projection.
rows.statement: Formalizes a four-stage chain separating Infinite Knowledge Space -> Information (via encounter/observation) -> Knowledge Capacity (via select/interpret/relate/evaluate) -> Knowledge Projection (within a defined scope), placing 'capacity' as an intermediate layer between the infinite space and any particular knowledge projection.

rows.anchor: what can be represented
rows.statement: Lists what Knowledge Capacity determines: what can be represented, what can be distinguished, what can be connected, what can be justified, what can be communicated, and what can be acted upon.

rows.anchor: Floridi gives us the idea that a representation is made at a selected **Level of Abstraction**, with a selected set of observables.
rows.statement: Ties the Knowledge Capacity construct back to all four prior book-lenses: Floridi's Level-of-Abstraction/observables defines what portion of a system can be represented; Gärdenfors' epistemic state contains commitments and changes through inputs/expansion/revision/contraction; Dretske separates information from its physical/linguistic encoding, so the capacity to 'write' information is not identical to the information itself; Searle adds that some information participates in institutional structures where context determines what something counts as.

rows.anchor: K = (B, L, R, C, P)
rows.statement: Formalizes Knowledge Capacity as the tuple K=(B,L,R,C,P) where B=boundary, L=level of abstraction, R=epistemic/reasoning regime, C=contextual capacity, P=participant/system capacity, producing a Knowledge Projection K(Omega) over the unbounded Knowledge Space Omega.
rows.type_signature: K = (B, L, R, C, P); Knowledge Projection = K(Omega)

rows.anchor: Knowledge is not only what is contained in the projection; it is also the capability and boundary that determine what can enter the projection.
rows.statement: States that knowledge is not only what is contained in a projection but also the capability and boundary that determine what can enter the projection in the first place.

rows.anchor: ## That gives us three different capacities
rows.statement: Distinguishes three separate capacities: (1) information capacity -- how much information can be captured or represented (storage, bandwidth, memory, sensor resolution); (2) epistemic capacity -- what the participant can distinguish, infer, justify, revise or understand (reasoning, awareness, inference, uncertainty handling, causal understanding); (3) expressive capacity -- what the participant can communicate or externalize (language, symbols, documents, models, code, diagrams).

rows.anchor:
high epistemic capacity
low expressive capacity
rows.statement: Gives worked capacity profiles illustrating the three-capacity distinction: a person may have high epistemic capacity but low expressive capacity, or high storage capacity but low epistemic capacity; an LLM may have high expressive capacity and large representational capacity but uncertain epistemic capacity; a database may have high preservation capacity but almost no intrinsic epistemic capacity.

rows.anchor: KnowledgeOS preserves and exposes the structures through which a participant can construct, scope, represent, evaluate, relate, revise, and communicate a projection of the infinite Knowledge Space.
rows.statement: Proposes a revised definition of KnowledgeOS, replacing 'KnowledgeOS stores knowledge' with 'KnowledgeOS preserves and exposes the structures through which a participant can construct, scope, represent, evaluate, relate, revise, and communicate a projection of the infinite Knowledge Space' -- concluding the Kernel does not need to contain 'knowledge' but needs to preserve the conditions and history of knowledge projection.

rows.anchor: Knowledge is a capacity to construct and maintain a bounded, meaningful projection of an unbounded Knowledge Space by selecting, relating, evaluating, preserving, and expressing information within a context and purpose.
rows.statement: Offers a further-refined single-sentence definition of knowledge: 'Knowledge is a capacity to construct and maintain a bounded, meaningful projection of an unbounded Knowledge Space by selecting, relating, evaluating, preserving, and expressing information within a context and purpose,' replacing the earlier 'capacity to write information and define the scope of information' formulation.

rows.anchor: Is 'capacity' itself a Kernel primitive, or is capacity derived from the participant, boundary, representation, epistemic regime, and available resources?
rows.statement: Leaves open whether 'capacity' itself is a Kernel primitive or is fully derived from participant + boundary + representation + epistemic regime + available resources, naming it the next question the Zero Lens should test.
dependencies: Zero Lens elimination test methodology (S0511, S0512)

lexical.anchor: What are we actually building when we say "KnowledgeOS"? ... None of these individually is "knowledge." ... our work has actually been a process of negative-space discovery ... what KnowledgeOS must not confuse with knowledge.

formal.anchor: KnowledgeOS Kernel should NOT contain "all knowledge" ... The Kernel should not own the world model. It should own the rules and structures that make a knowledge system trustworthy. ... The kernel is therefore closer to an epistemic infrastructure than a knowledge repository.

governance.anchor: I would NOT freeze this yet ... I would not create an ADR saying "this is the KnowledgeOS Kernel." Instead, I would create a discovery artifact: KOS — Kernel Boundary Discovery ... Semantic identity: Likely yes ... Word: No ... Knowledge state: Projection/hypothesis.

rationale_evidence.anchor: Not all projections are projections of the same kind of reality. Some project natural facts; some project semantic structures; some project institutional statuses; some project epistemic states.
rationale_evidence.statement: Refines the per-agent projection model (from S0529/S0530) by arguing not all projections project the same kind of reality -- some project natural facts, some semantic structures, some institutional statuses, some epistemic states -- and that KnowledgeOS must preserve which kind of projection a given projection is, calling this a major boundary condition.

sources.note: Step 105: tests Claude/Codex against the KnowledgeOS pointer-layer architecture. Notably contains several explicit FAIL experiments (not just PASS): duplicated agent-memory knowledge stores, an engineering rule embedded only in .claude/, incomplete agent-action attribution, incomplete recommendation provenance, a poorly-scoped agent-to-agent handoff, and Codex reading a superseded file directly instead of via KnowledgeOS -- named concrete failure modes. PASS material covers agent/KnowledgeOS layer separation, pointer-layer symmetry for Claude/Codex, agent attribution tuples, human-vs-agent authority (no self-authorization/inheritance), tool-level least privilege, context!=authority, agent knowledge-promotion lifecycle, three-way memory distinction, shared-knowledge convergence (Claude->K, Codex->K), a 5-layer non-overridable authority hierarchy grounding prompt-injection resistance, and full agent-action-assurance formalization.

rows.anchor: This is where our KnowledgeOS architecture meets Claude, Codex and other AI agents. Are the agents operating as governed engineering actors on top of KnowledgeOS, or are the agent harnesses themselves becoming parallel knowledge and governance systems?
rows.statement: Frames Step 105's central test: whether Claude/Codex operate as governed actors atop shared KnowledgeOS or have become parallel knowledge/governance systems.

rows.anchor: 105.1 — The fundamental boundary ... AgentBehavior ≠ EngineeringKnowledge. Agent layer defines how the agent operates (tools, permissions, workflow, safety, interaction behavior, local execution conventions). KnowledgeOS layer defines engineering knowledge, architecture, decisions, evidence, governa
rows.statement: Restates AgentBehavior ≠ EngineeringKnowledge as foundational, splitting the Agent layer (operating mechanics) from the KnowledgeOS layer (engineering knowledge/governance).

rows.anchor: 105.2 — The target architecture ... KnowledgeOS is shared. Agent harnesses are specialized.
rows.statement: Presents the target architecture diagram: KnowledgeOS shared at the top, Claude and Codex agents as specialized harnesses beneath it feeding Engineering Work.

rows.anchor: 105.3 — Experiment 1: duplicated knowledge ... .claude/memory/ contains an authoritative copy of architecture knowledge. .codex/memory/ contains another copy. Expected: KnowledgeDuplication=True, creating DivergenceRisk. Result: FAIL. This is an important failure mode.
rows.statement: Experiment 1: duplicated authoritative architecture knowledge across .claude/memory/ and .codex/memory/ creates DivergenceRisk; result FAIL — an important named failure mode the architecture must avoid, requiring pointer/index/agent-state directories rather than competing authoritative stores.

rows.anchor: 105.4 — Experiment 2: agent-specific operating rules ... .claude/ contains 'before modifying production configuration, require explicit confirmation.' This is agent behavior. Expected: AgentPolicy, not necessarily organizational architecture knowledge. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 2: an agent-behavior instruction in .claude/ correctly stays classified as AgentPolicy, not organizational knowledge; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 105.5 — Experiment 3: engineering rule hidden inside .claude/ ... 'All services must follow hexagonal architecture.' That is an engineering architecture rule. Expected: KnowledgeBoundaryViolation. Result: FAIL. The rule should be represented in the appropriate authoritative KnowledgeOS/governance ar
rows.statement: Experiment 3: an engineering architecture rule (hexagonal architecture requirement) existing only inside .claude/ is a KnowledgeBoundaryViolation; result FAIL — the rule must live in KnowledgeOS and be referenced, not embedded solely in agent configuration.

rows.anchor: 105.6 — The pointer-layer principle ... AgentHarness→KnowledgeOS rather than AgentHarness=KnowledgeOS. This is exactly why the earlier .claude / .codex symmetry matters.
rows.statement: Restates the pointer-layer principle AgentHarness→KnowledgeOS (never =), explaining why the .claude/.codex symmetry matters.

lineage_claims.quote: This is exactly why the earlier .claude / .codex symmetry matters.

rows.anchor: 105.7 — Experiment 4: Claude-specific knowledge ... Claude has a local instruction 'use Architecture Constitution v1.0.' KnowledgeOS contains the actual Constitution. Expected: valid pointer relationship Claude→Constitution_KnowledgeOS. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 4: Claude pointing to the KnowledgeOS-held Constitution rather than duplicating it is a valid pointer relationship; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 105.8 — Experiment 5: Codex-specific knowledge ... Codex uses 'Architecture Constitution v1.0' through its own operating instructions. Expected: same authoritative source Codex→Constitution_KnowledgeOS. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 5: Codex likewise pointing to the same authoritative Constitution_KnowledgeOS; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 105.9 — Symmetry does not mean identical configuration ... ClaudeConfig ≠ CodexConfig. That is perfectly valid. What must remain symmetric is the architectural boundary: AgentBehavior→SharedKnowledge.
rows.statement: States ClaudeConfig ≠ CodexConfig is valid; only the architectural AgentBehavior→SharedKnowledge boundary must remain symmetric.

rows.anchor: 105.10 — Experiment 6 ... Claude has .claude/settings.json. Codex has .codex/ with different configuration mechanisms. Expected: no architecture violation merely because configuration differs. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 6: differing configuration mechanisms between Claude and Codex is not itself an architecture violation; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 105.11 — Agent identity ... AgentAction=(AgentID,AgentVersion,Session,Actor,Tool,Action,Timestamp). This is necessary for assurance.
rows.statement: Defines the agent action attribution tuple AgentAction=(AgentID,AgentVersion,Session,Actor,Tool,Action,Timestamp).

type_signature.domain: AgentID x AgentVersion x Session x Actor x Tool x Action x Timestamp

rows.anchor: 105.12 — Experiment 7 ... Codex modifies a file. Audit record says only 'file changed.' No agent/session identity. Expected: incomplete attribution. Result: FAIL
rows.statement: Experiment 7: an audit record lacking agent/session identity for a file change is incomplete attribution; result FAIL.

rows.anchor: 105.13 — Agent identity versus human identity ... HumanActor from AgentActor. Human→Authorizes→Agent→Executes. This is different from Agent→SelfAuthorizes.
rows.statement: Distinguishes HumanActor from AgentActor, and Human→Authorizes→Agent→Executes from the forbidden Agent→SelfAuthorizes.

rows.anchor: 105.14 — Experiment 8 ... Developer asks Codex to perform a migration. Codex executes it. Expected trace: Developer→AgentRequest→Codex→Action. Result: PASS provided the authorization semantics are preserved.
rows.statement: Experiment 8: a developer-requested migration executed by Codex must trace Developer→AgentRequest→Codex→Action with preserved authorization semantics; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 105.15 — Agent does not inherit unlimited human authority ... If HumanAuthority=A, it does not automatically follow that AgentAuthority=A. The agent's authority should be explicitly bounded.
rows.statement: States HumanAuthority=A does not imply AgentAuthority=A; agent authority must be explicitly bounded.

rows.anchor: 105.16 — Experiment 9 ... Developer is authorized to approve architecture changes. Developer tells Codex 'approve this for me.' Expected: Codex cannot simply inherit the developer's approval authority unless explicitly designed and authorized to act as delegate. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 9: Codex cannot inherit a developer's approval authority merely by being asked, absent explicit delegate authorization; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 105.17 — Tool authority ... ToolPermission(agent,tool,scope). ReadRepository=True, WriteRepository=True, DeployProduction=False.
rows.statement: Defines per-tool authority ToolPermission(agent,tool,scope), e.g. ReadRepository=True/WriteRepository=True/DeployProduction=False.

rows.anchor: 105.18 — Experiment 10 ... Codex has repository write access but no production deployment permission. Expected: repository modification Allowed, production deployment Denied. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 10: Codex's differentiated tool permissions (repo write allowed, production deploy denied) function correctly; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 105.19 — Least privilege ... AgentAuthority = MinimumNecessaryAuthority. This should apply separately to filesystem, Git, CI/CD, databases, cloud, production, secrets, external APIs.
rows.statement: States AgentAuthority = MinimumNecessaryAuthority (least privilege), applied per resource category (filesystem/Git/CI-CD/databases/cloud/production/secrets/external APIs).

rows.anchor: 105.20 — Agent context ... Context ≠ Authority. An agent may know 'production deployment is allowed after approval' without itself being authorized to approve.
rows.statement: States Context ≠ Authority: knowing a policy does not confer authority to act on it.

rows.anchor: 105.21 — Experiment 11 ... Agent retrieves the production deployment policy. Expected: knowledge access does not imply deployment authority. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 11: retrieving a deployment policy does not confer deployment authority; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 105.22 — Context provenance ... when an agent receives knowledge, it should know Where, When, Version, Authority, Confidence. Otherwise the agent may reason over stale or non-authoritative information.
rows.statement: States retrieved context needs Where/When/Version/Authority/Confidence to prevent reasoning over stale or non-authoritative information.

rows.anchor: 105.23 — Experiment 12 ... Claude retrieves an architecture rule. KnowledgeOS returns RuleVersion=1.0. Current rule is 1.2. Expected: Claude should be able to detect that the knowledge is stale. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 12: Claude must be able to detect a retrieved rule (1.0) is stale relative to the current version (1.2); result PASS.

rows.anchor: 105.24 — Agent reasoning provenance ... Recommendation→EvidenceUsed and ideally Recommendation→ReasoningContext. The exact internal chain-of-thought need not be exposed or persisted. What matters is decision-relevant provenance, not private chain-of-thought.
rows.statement: Distinguishes required decision-relevant provenance (Recommendation→EvidenceUsed/ReasoningContext) from unnecessary private chain-of-thought.

rows.anchor: 105.25 — Experiment 13 ... Claude recommends 'use architecture option B.' No evidence references are retained. Expected: recommendation provenance is incomplete. Result: FAIL
rows.statement: Experiment 13: a Claude recommendation with no retained evidence references has incomplete recommendation provenance; result FAIL.

rows.anchor: 105.26 — We do not need to store private reasoning ... KnowledgeOS should preserve Evidence, RelevantSources, DecisionRationale, Outcome. It does not need to become a repository for hidden model reasoning.
rows.statement: States KnowledgeOS must preserve Evidence/RelevantSources/DecisionRationale/Outcome, not become a repository of hidden model reasoning.

rows.anchor: 105.27 — Agent recommendation ... KnowledgeOSContext→AgentReasoning→Recommendation. Then Recommendation→Human/GovernanceDecision.
rows.statement: Defines the agent recommendation lifecycle KnowledgeOSContext→AgentReasoning→Recommendation→Human/GovernanceDecision.

rows.anchor: 105.28 — Experiment 14 ... Claude recommends changing an architecture boundary. Architecture Board approves. Expected: Recommendation→Decision. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 14: a Claude recommendation approved by the Architecture Board correctly becomes Recommendation→Decision; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 105.29 — Autonomous engineering action ... RunTests. A pre-authorized agent may execute TestExecution. Autonomy ≠ Forbidden. The requirement is Autonomy ⊆ AuthorizedPolicy.
rows.statement: States Autonomy ≠ Forbidden but requires Autonomy ⊆ AuthorizedPolicy, e.g. pre-authorized test execution.

rows.anchor: 105.30 — Experiment 15 ... Codex automatically runs unit tests after modifying code. Policy permits it. Expected: AuthorizedAutonomy. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 15: Codex's policy-permitted automatic unit test execution is AuthorizedAutonomy; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 105.31 — High-risk action ... DeployProduction should generally have a stronger authorization requirement than RunUnitTests. Risk(Action)→RequiredControlLevel.
rows.statement: Defines Risk(Action)→RequiredControlLevel, requiring stronger authorization for higher-risk actions like DeployProduction vs RunUnitTests.

rows.anchor: 105.32 — Experiment 16 ... Agent automatically deploys production after a failed verification. Expected: Blocked. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 16: an agent must be Blocked from automatically deploying to production after failed verification; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 105.33 — Agent action ledger ... AgentSession→Requests→ToolCalls→Changes→Verification→Outcome. This becomes the agent equivalent of the governance evidence chain.
rows.statement: Defines the agent action ledger AgentSession→Requests→ToolCalls→Changes→Verification→Outcome, the agent analogue of the governance evidence chain.

rows.anchor: 105.34 — Experiment 17 ... Agent changes three files. One test fails. Expected: the action history connects Change→FailedTest. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 17: an agent's action history must connect a code change to a resulting FailedTest; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 105.35 — Agent-generated knowledge ... AgentObservation→Evidence. But AgentGeneratedClaim must retain its origin.
rows.statement: Defines AgentObservation→Evidence, with AgentGeneratedClaim required to retain its agent origin.

rows.anchor: 105.36 — Experiment 18 ... Codex discovers an undocumented dependency. Expected: Observation→Evidence→CandidateKnowledge. Not automatically AuthoritativeArchitectureFact. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 18: an agent's discovery becomes Observation→Evidence→CandidateKnowledge, not automatically an authoritative fact; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 105.37 — Agent knowledge promotion ... Candidate→Reviewed→Verified→Authoritative. This is especially useful for AI-generated discoveries.
rows.statement: Defines the four-stage knowledge-promotion lifecycle Candidate→Reviewed→Verified→Authoritative for AI-generated discoveries.

rows.anchor: 105.38 — Experiment 19 ... Claude proposes 'Service X is a bounded context.' Expected: CandidateClassification. Human/domain review may promote it. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 19: a Claude-proposed bounded-context classification is CandidateClassification pending human/domain review; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 105.39 — Agent memory ... Ephemeral context (current task/session), Agent state (operational info), Organizational knowledge (authoritative engineering knowledge). These are different.
rows.statement: Distinguishes three non-collapsible memory categories: Ephemeral context, Agent state, Organizational knowledge.

rows.anchor: 105.40 — Experiment 20 ... Claude stores 'user prefers concise output.' This is agent/user interaction state. It should not become ArchitectureKnowledge. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 20: user-preference interaction state must never be promoted to ArchitectureKnowledge; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 105.41 — Knowledge promotion boundary ... AgentMemory→CandidateKnowledge→GovernedKnowledge. Promotion requires appropriate validation.
rows.statement: Defines the promotion pipeline AgentMemory→CandidateKnowledge→GovernedKnowledge requiring validation.

rows.anchor: 105.42 — Experiment 21 ... Claude remembers 'we decided to use PostgreSQL.' But no decision record exists. Expected: memory cannot automatically become authoritative organizational knowledge. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 21: an unrecorded remembered decision cannot automatically become authoritative organizational knowledge; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 105.43 — Claude and Codex must converge on the same truth ... Claude retrieves ArchitectureRule_1.2. Codex retrieves ArchitectureRule_1.1. Expected: KnowledgeOS should identify the version discrepancy. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 22 (implicit): KnowledgeOS must identify a version discrepancy when Claude and Codex retrieve different rule versions (1.2 vs 1.1); result PASS.

rows.anchor: 105.44 — The shared knowledge principle ... Claude→K and Codex→K where K is the governed KnowledgeOS knowledge state. This is much stronger than Claude↔Codex through copied memory.
rows.statement: States the shared-knowledge principle Claude→K and Codex→K (both converging on one governed state K), strictly stronger than direct Claude↔Codex memory-copy synchronization.

rows.anchor: 105.45 — Agent-to-agent communication ... Claude→Codex handoff should preserve Context, Task, Authorization, Evidence, ExpectedOutcome.
rows.statement: Defines required handoff fields for agent-to-agent communication: Context, Task, Authorization, Evidence, ExpectedOutcome.

rows.anchor: 105.46 — Experiment 22 ... Claude tells Codex 'fix the architecture.' Codex has no defined scope or evidence. Expected: poorly governed handoff. Result: FAIL
rows.statement: Experiment: a vague Claude-to-Codex handoff ('fix the architecture') lacking scope/evidence is a poorly governed handoff; result FAIL.

rows.anchor: 105.47 — Better handoff ... Task: FixViolation(X). Evidence: ArchitectureFinding(Y). Scope: RepositoryZ. Authority: ApprovedChange123. Now Codex can act within a defined boundary.
rows.statement: Provides a corrected handoff example with explicit Task/Evidence/Scope/Authority fields enabling Codex to act within a defined boundary.

rows.anchor: 105.48 — Experiment 23 ... Claude generates a remediation task from a verified finding. Codex executes it. Expected: Finding→Task→Action→Verification. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment: a well-formed Finding→Task→Action→Verification handoff chain executes correctly; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 105.49 — Agent architecture as a control plane ... KnowledgeOS = Shared Semantic Control Plane for Agents and Engineering. Claude and Codex are execution/reasoning participants.
rows.statement: States KnowledgeOS = Shared Semantic Control Plane for agents and engineering, with Claude/Codex as execution/reasoning participants.

rows.anchor: 105.50 — The dangerous alternative ... Claude and Codex each with private memory, private rules, private architecture interpretation. This eventually creates KnowledgeFragmentation.
rows.statement: Warns that independent private memory/rules/interpretation per agent eventually creates KnowledgeFragmentation.

rows.anchor: 105.51 — Desired architecture ... KnowledgeOS at the center, with Claude, Codex, Human all connected to it, feeding Engineering. The knowledge boundary is centralized conceptually, even if physically distributed.
rows.statement: Presents the desired centralized-conceptually architecture: KnowledgeOS at the hub connecting Claude/Codex/Human, feeding Engineering.

rows.anchor: 105.52 — 'Centralized' needs qualification ... KnowledgeOS does not necessarily mean OneDatabase. It means OneAuthoritativeSemanticModel. Physical storage can remain distributed.
rows.statement: Clarifies 'centralized' KnowledgeOS means OneAuthoritativeSemanticModel, not OneDatabase — physical storage may remain distributed.

rows.anchor: 105.53 — Experiment 24 ... Evidence in object storage, metadata in PostgreSQL, architecture artifacts in Git, runtime events in an observability platform. Expected: still valid if KnowledgeOS maintains the semantic relationships and authority across them. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment: physically distributed storage (object storage/PostgreSQL/Git/observability platform) remains valid KnowledgeOS as long as semantic relationships and authority are maintained across it; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 105.54 — Agent tool boundary ... Agents should not bypass KnowledgeOS where governed knowledge is required. Agent→RandomFile instead of Agent→KnowledgeOS may produce inconsistent context.
rows.statement: States agents must not bypass KnowledgeOS for governed knowledge (Agent→RandomFile instead of Agent→KnowledgeOS produces inconsistent context).

rows.anchor: 105.55 — Experiment 25 ... Codex reads an old architecture Markdown file directly while current KnowledgeOS knowledge has superseded it. Expected: potential stale-context violation. Result: FAIL. The architecture should establish how authoritative current knowledge is retrieved.
