Tuning τ to obtain the 'expected' answer would have been exactly the make-the-model-work-by-construction the protocol forbids.
rows.statement: Explicit methodological discipline: when the protocol's CASE 1 (expecting unique determination from 100 candidates) instead returned 2 admissible candidates, the result was diagnosed (computed why via false-admission probability at different thresholds) rather than tuned away -- refusing to adjust the threshold merely to match the expected answer, which the protocol's own discipline forbids.

rows.anchor: Applying a multiplicity-corrected (Bonferroni) admissibility threshold, signal=0.6, m=40: n=100 τ=0.520 truth admissible ✔ ... n=1000 τ=0.615 truth admissible ✘ -- the truth is EXCLUDED ... Candidate count and evidence quantity are coupled. At fixed evidence, a real signal of 0.6 becomes inadmissible somewhere between n=100 and n=1000.
rows.statement: [EXP] NEW result: candidate count and evidence quantity are statistically coupled -- applying a Bonferroni multiplicity-corrected admissibility threshold at fixed evidence (m=40), a genuine signal of 0.6 remains admissible through n=100 but becomes excluded (the truth is wrongly rejected) between n=100 and n=1000, with the required evidence m growing as 2 ln n to restore admissibility.

experiment.hypothesis: Increasing candidate count at fixed evidence eventually makes a genuine signal statistically inadmissible under a sound multiplicity-corrected threshold
experiment.setup: Bonferroni-corrected admissibility threshold tau=z(1-alpha/n)*sigma/sqrt(m), fixed signal=0.6, m=40
experiment.assumptions: standard normal-approximation extreme-value bound z^2~2 ln n
experiment.method: compute z(1-alpha/n), the resulting threshold tau at m=40, and whether the true signal (0.6) exceeds tau
experiment.result: truth admissible for n<=100 (tau up to 0.520) but excluded for n>=1000 (tau>=0.615); m required to restore admissibility grows from 8 (n=1) to 67 (n=100000)
experiment.interpretation: more candidates does not merely fail to help -- at fixed evidence it actively destroys the ability to detect a real signal; no threshold is simultaneously sound against multiplicity and sensitive to a fixed signal as n grows
experiment.limitations: depends on the specific normal-approximation model and Bonferroni correction choice
experiment.conclusion: [EXP] sharpens H1: this is worse than merely 'no improvement'

rows.anchor: CORRECTED -- scope of the remedy. This section originally concluded 'the fix is evidence, not thresholds.' Directionally right, too absolute. ... multiplicity control cannot be obtained for free. The admissible remedies include more evidence, stronger prior or structural constraints, multiplicity-aware inference, reduced effective hypothesis complexity, hierarchical modelling, replication, and independent evidence -- this experiment tested only the first.
rows.statement: Explicit self-correction: walks back an original overclaim ('the fix is evidence, not thresholds') to the narrower, correct statement that multiplicity control cannot be obtained for free and has at least seven possible remedies (more evidence, stronger priors/structural constraints, multiplicity-aware inference, reduced effective hypothesis complexity, hierarchical modelling, replication, independent evidence), of which only the first was actually tested.

rows.anchor: false proportion measured, never assumed: G1/G2/G5/G6 = 1.000; G3 correlated = 1.000 diversity 0.200 (1000/200 independent groups); G4 near-duplicate = 1.000 diversity 0.050 (1000/50); G7 mostly-true = 0.200. H12 confirmed. The false proportion ranges 0.20 → 1.00 across generators. ... candidate count ≠ candidate diversity: G4 offers 1000 candidates and 50 independent alternatives.
rows.statement: [NEG]/[EXP] H12 confirmed: measured (not assumed) false-hypothesis proportion ranges from 0.20 to 1.00 across seven generator types, refuting any universal 'most hypotheses are false' claim; additionally candidate count != candidate diversity (G4 near-duplicate: 1000 candidates but only 50 independent alternative groups, G3 correlated: 1000 candidates but 200 independent groups) -- any 'we considered a thousand hypotheses' argument must separately report diversity.

experiment.hypothesis: H12: the biological million-to-one false-hypothesis ratio has no universal epistemological status
experiment.setup: seven candidate generators (G1 random, G2 diverse, G3 correlated, G4 near-duplicate, G5 adversarial, G6 mostly-false, G7 mostly-true), n=1000 candidates each
experiment.assumptions: none; false proportion measured directly against evaluator-only ground truth
experiment.method: measure false proportion and diversity (independent-group count) per generator
experiment.result: false proportion 1.000 for G1/G2/G5/G6, 1.000 for G3/G4 (but with diversity 0.200/0.050 respectively), 0.200 for G7
experiment.interpretation: the false-hypothesis rate is a property of the generator, not a law of epistemology; diversity and count are distinct measured quantities
experiment.limitations: four generators producing exactly 1.000 false proportion never emit the truth by construction, so this is a designed rather than emergent extreme
experiment.conclusion: [NEG] H12 confirmed; also confirms candidate-count!=diversity

rows.anchor: a generator that cannot produce the truth is a real epistemic failure mode, and it makes |A_t|=0 the correct outcome (H7).
rows.statement: Notes that a generator which never emits the truth (four of seven tested) is a genuine epistemic failure mode in its own right, and correctly produces |A_t|=0 as the right outcome (confirming H7), not a measurement defect.

rows.anchor: Pareto/admissibility: |A|=9 -- incomparability preserved, both survivors retained. scalar argmax: |A|=1 -- unique by construction. threshold τ=0.5: |A|=1. ... 'Best candidate' is a consequence of the imposed scoring function, not a property of the candidate set.
rows.statement: [EXP] H8 confirmed: with candidates constructed to be genuinely incomparable (H_true stronger on evidence+explanatory power, H_twin stronger on consistency), Pareto/admissibility selection preserves incomparability (|A|=9 survivors) while scalar argmax and threshold selection both force a unique winner (|A|=1) purely as an artifact of the scoring function -- 'best candidate' is manufactured by the ranking method, not discovered in the candidate set.

experiment.hypothesis: H8: a total scalar ranking manufactures uniqueness rather than discovering it
experiment.setup: candidates with genuine multi-dimensional incomparability (H_true better on evidence+explanatory power, H_twin better on consistency)
experiment.assumptions: Pareto/admissibility, scalar argmax, and threshold (tau=0.5) selection methods are compared on the same candidate set
experiment.method: apply each selection method and record |A| (surviving candidate count)
experiment.result: Pareto/admissibility: |A|=9; scalar argmax: |A|=1; threshold: |A|=1
experiment.interpretation: uniqueness under scalar/threshold methods is an artifact of the scoring function, not evidence of a true unique best candidate
experiment.conclusion: [EXP] H8 confirmed

rows.anchor: H5 unique survivor ⇏ Knowledge confirmed. H6 multiple survivors can be correct confirmed -- |A|=5 in the observationally-equivalent world. H7 zero survivors can be correct confirmed -- |A|=0 in the none-admissible world. H2 candidate reduction ≠ epistemic progress confirmed both directions -- ρ=0.999 with no quality gain in the null world; ρ=0.1 that removed the one decisively refuted candidate.
rows.statement: Confirms H5 (unique survivor does not imply Knowledge), H6 (multiple survivors, |A|=5, can be the correct outcome in an observationally-equivalent world), H7 (zero survivors, |A|=0, can be correct in a none-admissible world), and H2 in both directions (a candidate-reduction rate of 0.999 accompanies zero quality gain in the null world, while a low reduction rate of 0.1 can still remove the one decisively refuted candidate) -- CandidateReduction (rho=1-|H_{t+1}|/|H_t|) is confirmed to be neither KnowledgeGain nor EpistemicProgress.

rows.anchor: World W4: decoy signal 0.9, truth signal 0.3 ... selected (best apparent fit): H_decoy ... independent held-out validation of the selected: 0.9849 → PASSES ... ground truth: H_true [evaluator only]. Selection and validation AGREED -- and both were wrong. This is stronger than 'Selection ≠ Validation.'
rows.statement: [NEG], a result stronger than H3: constructs world W4 with a decoy hypothesis carrying genuinely higher evidential signal (0.9) than the true hypothesis (0.3, still H_true); selection picks the decoy on best apparent fit, and independent held-out validation on the same evidence channel also passes the decoy (0.9849) -- selection and validation agree and are both wrong, since the decoy's advantage is real within that evidence channel, not an artifact detectable by more validation on the same channel.

experiment.hypothesis: Selection agreeing with independent validation is sufficient to trust the selected candidate
experiment.setup: world W4 with a decoy hypothesis (signal 0.9) and the true hypothesis H_true (signal 0.3), ground truth evaluator-only
experiment.assumptions: validation uses the same evidence channel as selection
experiment.inputs: decoy and H_true signals on one evidence channel
experiment.method: select best apparent fit, then independently validate the selected candidate on held-out data from the same channel
experiment.result: decoy is selected and passes held-out validation (0.9849) despite H_true being ground truth
experiment.interpretation: validation confined to the same misleading evidence channel cannot detect channel-level bias; a genuinely independent channel or intervention might change the conclusion (tested in a following section)
experiment.limitations: scope explicitly corrected from an original unbounded claim to this channel-specific one
experiment.conclusion: [NEG] recorded as factivity unresolved, not repaired

rows.anchor: Validation confined to the same misleading evidence channel cannot detect channel-level bias. (Scope corrected: the original wording -- 'validation cannot repair a misleading evidence channel' -- was unbounded. With a genuinely independent channel E1⊥E2, or an intervention do(X=x), the conclusion may change.) Recorded as factivity unresolved; not repaired here.
rows.statement: Second explicit self-correction in this document: narrows an originally unbounded claim ('validation cannot repair a misleading evidence channel') to the channel-specific claim that validation confined to the same misleading channel cannot detect channel-level bias, noting a genuinely independent channel or a causal intervention might change the conclusion; recorded as factivity unresolved, deliberately not repaired within this experiment.

rows.anchor: Reconstructing set-valued Sel using only existing v1.2 capabilities -- Validate (warrant threshold) + Discriminate (pairwise dominance) + Determine (set-valued admissibility): agreement with Sel on 200/200 random configurations. Outcome A -- REDUNDANCY. Selection = f(Discriminate, Validate, Determine), reproduced exactly. The candidate-multiplicity model introduces no new irreducible kernel capability.
rows.statement: [EXP] H11 confirmed, kernel test outcome A (Redundancy): the set-valued Selection operator is reconstructed exactly (200/200 agreement on random configurations) from three existing v1.2 capabilities -- Validate (warrant threshold), Discriminate (pairwise dominance), and Determine (set-valued admissibility) -- so the candidate-multiplicity model introduces no new irreducible kernel capability.

experiment.hypothesis: H11: if existing operations reproduce Selection's behavior, no new kernel primitive is justified
experiment.setup: implement Selection as f(Discriminate,Validate,Determine) using existing v1.2 capability definitions
experiment.assumptions: the three chosen existing operators are correctly implemented per v1.2 semantics
experiment.method: compare the composed f(Discriminate,Validate,Determine) output against the direct Sel implementation on each configuration
experiment.result: 200/200 agreement
experiment.interpretation: Selection is derivable (redundant), not an irreducible kernel primitive
experiment.limitations: establishes derivability of the set-valued operation only; does not refute Selection being a distinct DDD responsibility (outcome B untested); no kernel minimality claim is admissible while semantic equivalence is undefined; Select was not assumed primitive merely from its name
experiment.conclusion: [EXP] outcome A: redundancy

rows.anchor: Twelve of twelve SUPPORTED UNDER THE TESTED SCENARIOS. None refuted. (Status corrected: supported, not established...) That is a weak outcome by this programme's standards ... The two genuinely new results are §2 (multiplicity-evidence coupling) and §6 (validation agreeing with a wrong selection), and neither was among the twelve.
rows.statement: Final tally: all twelve hypotheses (H1-H12) are supported under the tested scenarios and none refuted, explicitly downgraded from 'established' to 'supported' as a third self-correction (confirmation under one experimental model is not theory-level establishment); notes this is judged a 'weak' outcome by the programme's own standard since the hypotheses were well-chosen and unsurprising -- the genuinely novel results (multiplicity-evidence coupling, section 2; selection-validation agreeing while both wrong, section 6) were not among the pre-specified twelve.

rows.anchor: Theory amendments -- none proposed. a Selection kernel primitive: outcome A, derivable. a candidate-count parameter in S^epi: justified by §2, but presupposes ⪰; recorded [OPEN], not proposed. Linga/Yoni structure: [EXT]; nothing in the experiment establishes it. No v1.3. ... Admissibility must be a function of candidate count ... Formulating that requires the ordering -- the same blocker as L5 and the stagnation predicate. Do not conclude from outcome A that Select should be removed from the operator vocabulary. Derivable ≠ mergeable.
rows.statement: No theory amendment is proposed despite the strong results: a Selection kernel primitive is rejected (derivable), a candidate-count parameter in S^epi is justified by section 2 but left [OPEN] since it presupposes the epistemic-status ordering, and Linga/Yoni remains [EXT]; baseline stays v1.2. Adds 'admissibility must be a function of candidate count' [PROP] to the ordering-blocked queue, and explicitly warns not to conclude Select should be removed from the operator vocabulary merely because it is derivable (derivable != mergeable).

rows.anchor: P(detect decoy | same channel)=0.0075 versus P(detect decoy | independent channel)=0.9928. ... Validation Independence must be defined relative to the evidence channel. ... ValidationContext=(Channel, Evidence, Model, Population, Time, Standard,...). ... Channel_selection ≠ Channel_validation is one possible requirement for independent validation.
rows.statement: Highlights a follow-up validation-channel test showing decoy detection probability jumps from 0.0075 (same channel as selection) to 0.9928 (independent channel) -- confirming validation independence must be defined relative to the evidence channel, proposing a candidate ValidationContext=(Channel,Evidence,Model,Population,Time,Standard,...) tuple with Channel_selection!=Channel_validation as one possible independent-validation requirement.

rows.anchor: every validation step must declare its evidence channel. I would adopt this as a candidate architectural/schema rule, but keep the distinction: channel declaration ≠ channel independence. ... ChannelRelation(c_1,c_2) with possibilities such as: same, independent under stated assumptions, partially dependent, unknown, causally coupled.
rows.statement: Endorses mandatory declaration of a validation step's evidence channel as a candidate schema rule, while distinguishing channel declaration from channel independence (a declaration only states Channel(V)=c, not Independent(Channel(V),Channel(S))), proposing a richer ChannelRelation(c1,c2) taxonomy: same, independent-under-stated-assumptions, partially dependent, unknown, or causally coupled.

rows.anchor: selection cannot be evaluated independently of the structure of the candidate space and evidence channels. So perhaps the real object isn't: Select(H) but something more like: Select(H,E,M,S,Λ) where Λ captures the relevant hypothesis-space/evidence structure. Again: [PROP], not theory.
rows.statement: Proposes extending Selection's signature from Select(H) to Select(H,E,M,S,Lambda) where Lambda captures the relevant hypothesis-space/evidence structure, since selection cannot be evaluated independently of candidate-space dependence structure -- explicitly [PROP], not theory.

rows.anchor: many candidates → {0,1,>1} and: more candidates ⇏ better outcome. ... candidate dependence changes the epistemic burden. So the useful abstraction from the metaphor is now: Multiplicity + competition + dependence + selection pressure -- not 'millions produce the best one.'
rows.statement: Updates the 'Linga's Millions' metaphor's useful abstraction in light of the M2O and NEFF results: not 'millions produce the best one' but 'multiplicity + competition + dependence + selection pressure', since outcomes can be 0/1/>1 survivors and candidate dependence materially changes epistemic burden.

rows.anchor: same (misleading) channel: detects the decoy 0.0075. independent channel: detects the decoy 0.9928. ... Channel independence does the work, not validation per se. ... REFINED -- declaration is not independence. Channel(V)=c is a declaration; it does not establish Independent(Channel(V),Channel(S)). ... ChannelRelation(c1,c2) ∈ {same, independent-under-stated-assumptions, partially-dependent, unknown, causally-coupled}.
rows.statement: [EXP]: over 4000 trials, validating on the same (misleading) channel as selection detects a decoy in only 0.75% of trials, while validating on an independent channel detects it in 99.28% -- confirming channel independence, not validation per se, is what does the epistemic work; refines the resulting design principle to distinguish channel declaration (Channel(V)=c) from channel independence (a genuine ChannelRelation(c1,c2) taxonomy: same / independent-under-stated-assumptions / partially-dependent / unknown / causally-coupled), feeding a candidate ValidationContext=(Channel,Evidence,Model,Population,Time,Standard,...) object, [PROP] supported not adopted.

experiment.hypothesis: Validating a selected candidate on an independent evidence channel detects a decoy that same-channel validation misses
experiment.setup: world with a decoy (misleadingly strong signal) and true hypothesis; validate on same vs independent channel, 4000 trials
experiment.assumptions: an independent channel genuinely carries different information about the decoy
experiment.inputs: decoy/truth signal configuration from the parent M2O experiment's world W4
experiment.method: run 4000 trials of same-channel vs independent-channel validation, measure decoy detection rate
experiment.result: same-channel detection 0.75%, independent-channel detection 99.28%
experiment.interpretation: channel independence is the operative property, not the act of validation itself
experiment.conclusion: [EXP] confirmed, scope-bounded

rows.anchor: H_Q → EvidenceAssessment → Determination → KnowledgeAttribution. And determination may be: |𝒜_Q|=0, |𝒜_Q|=1, |𝒜_Q|>1. So the system can legitimately conclude: 'There are several admissible explanations; the evidence does not determine one.' That is much more rigorous than forcing a winner.
rows.statement: Lists the determination layer (Hypotheses->EvidenceAssessment->Determination->KnowledgeAttribution, with cardinality 0/1/>1 outcomes) as stable, allowing the system to legitimately report multiple admissible explanations rather than being forced to pick a winner.

rows.anchor: The Linga-Yoni experiment showed that generation ≠ progress. A system can change without improving.
rows.statement: Restates a finding attributed to the (prior-batch) Linga-Yoni experiment: generation is not progress — a system can change state without that change constituting improvement, motivating the need for an explicit progress ordering.

lexical.anchor: Claim A: 'Knowledge = one selected proposal.' Reject. ... A selected hypothesis can be false. This is exactly the unresolved factivity problem. So: P* = Select(𝓗) does not imply: Knows(P*). At most: Accepted(P*).

formal.anchor: 𝓗_t → Assessment_t → 𝒜_t → Transformation_t where 𝓗_t = candidate hypothesis space, Assessment_t = evaluation of candidates, 𝒜_t ⊆ 𝓗_t = surviving/admissible candidates, Transformation_t = construction of the resulting epistemic product/state.

operational.anchor: KR-M2O-2026-09-02 -- Candidate Multiplicity and Selection. Test: Generate N hypotheses. Vary N: 1,10,100,1000,10000. Apply identical evidence. Measure: candidate reduction, unique determination rate, false-selection rate, validation failure rate, hypothesis diversity, dependence between candidates. ... H0: More candidate generation does not necessarily improve epistemic quality. I strongly suspect this will survive.

governance.anchor: Candidate Multiplicity is not a nuisance; it is a mathematical dimension of epistemic systems. ... generation → competition → assessment → selection → validation → determination → attribution. That is a genuine candidate extension of the theory. But I would not amend Theory v1.2 yet. First run the candidate-multiplicity experiment.

rationale_evidence.anchor: H_1 has stronger evidence but poorer explanatory power, while H_2 has stronger explanatory power but weaker evidence. Neither may dominate. Then: H_1 ⋡ H_2 and: H_2 ⋡ H_1. Therefore both survive: 𝒜_Q={H_1,H_2}. ... The Linga's Millions model has accidentally brought us directly to one of our existing theoretical bottlenecks [⪰].
rationale_evidence.statement: Argues for a partial order over hypotheses rather than a scalar 'best' score: two hypotheses with incomparable strengths (H1 stronger evidence/weaker explanatory power, H2 vice versa) neither dominates the other under a partial order, so both survive in the admissible set -- directly implicating the still-undefined epistemic-status ordering (>=) as this document's central bottleneck too.

rationale_evidence.anchor: If you generate millions of hypotheses and then select the strongest-performing one, you can get max_i Score(H_i) that looks impressive even when all candidates are noise. This is the statistical phenomenon of selection / multiple comparisons / winner's curse. So: Best observed candidate ≠ Best underlying hypothesis.
rationale_evidence.statement: Introduces the statistical selection-bias/multiple-comparisons/winner's-curse phenomenon into KnowledgeOS: selecting the best-scoring candidate from a large generated set can look impressive even when all candidates are pure noise, establishing 'best observed candidate != best underlying hypothesis' -- directly relevant to AI systems generating thousands of candidate explanations and picking the best apparent fit (best overfit).

rationale_evidence.anchor: H* = argmax_H S_train(H) does not imply: H* = argmax_H S_future(H). Therefore KnowledgeOS should distinguish: Selection Evidence ≠ Validation Evidence.
rationale_evidence.statement: Formalizes the anti-overfitting principle: the hypothesis maximizing training-evidence score need not maximize future/validation-evidence score, giving the architectural distinction Selection Evidence != Validation Evidence.

rationale_evidence.anchor: a generator that cannot produce the truth is a real epistemic failure mode, and it makes |A_t|=0 the correct outcome (H7).
rationale_evidence.statement: Notes that a generator which never emits the truth (four of seven tested) is a genuine epistemic failure mode in its own right, and correctly produces |A_t|=0 as the right outcome (confirming H7), not a measurement defect.

sources.note: A 29-section implementation-ready experiment prompt for KR-BRIDGE-01-ZERO-PRESERVATION-2026-09: the first bridge/falsification experiment explicitly testing whether Transformation-relative Zero and representation-preservation adequacy are related, using an independently-generated parallel (non-sequential) representation family, a four-hypothesis (H0-H3) and four-cell Zero x Adequacy crossing design, T x Pi interaction testing, six controls, ten falsification questions (Q1-Q10), four outcome classes (A absent / B conditional / C robust / D design failure), mandated audit and results artifacts at verification/zero-algebra/KR-BRIDGE-01-*-2026-09.md, and strict governance immutability constraints on Theory v1.2 and all prior historical results.

rows.anchor: EXPERIMENT ID KR-BRIDGE-01-ZERO-PRESERVATION-2026-09 ... Determine whether there is any reproducible empirical or structural relationship between: A. elimination/Transformation-relative Zero, B. representation preservation/adequacy. WITHOUT assuming that Zero is a preservation criterion. ... The exp
rows.statement: Commissions KR-BRIDGE-01-ZERO-PRESERVATION-2026-09, a bridge/falsification experiment explicitly designed to determine whether there is any reproducible relationship between elimination/Transformation-relative Zero and representation-preservation adequacy without assuming Zero is a preservation criterion, required to remain capable of falsifying the hypothesized relationship, and prohibited from constructing an algebra, pre-selecting a carrier, modifying Theory v1.2, creating Theory v1.3, selecting a kernel operator, or merging KR-ZERO and KR-REP-REDUCTION into one formalism.

rows.anchor: KR-ZERO: ~89.7% singleton-determined levels ... ~8.2% irreducible levels ... Does NOT establish Zero as a preservation criterion. KR-REP-REDUCTION: R5 adequate, R4 inadequate ... Found no observed Zero/boundary association in that experiment. Does NOT establish a KR-ZERO law. ... These experiments a
rows.statement: Summarizes the existing empirical baseline the bridge experiment builds on: KR-ZERO (89.7% singleton-determined, 8.2% irreducible, does not establish Zero as a preservation criterion) and KR-REP-REDUCTION (R5 adequate/R4 inadequate, no observed Zero/boundary association), framed as complementary but analytically independent results whose missing bridge the new experiment must test rather than assume.

rows.anchor: H0: Zero and preservation are not systematically related in the tested regime. H1: Zero is associated with preservation under specified conditions. H2: Zero is predictive of preservation only under particular transformation/observable/contract configurations. H3: Any apparent relationship is explain
rows.statement: Specifies four competing hypotheses to be distinguished -- H0 no systematic relationship, H1 association under specified conditions, H2 predictive only under particular transformation/observable/contract configurations, H3 apparent relationship explained by a confounding factor (transformation class, contract, observable, redundancy, representation regime) -- with an explicit instruction not to privilege H1, and defines success as producing a clear positive or negative result regarding the tested relationship.

rows.anchor: USE A PARALLEL REPRESENTATION FAMILY. Do NOT use only a deterministic sequential chain. A sequential chain ... has a data-processing constraint H(Q|Rn) <= H(Q|R(n-1)) and therefore cannot test non-monotone adequacy. The present experiment requires independently generated representations: Ra = Ta(D),
rows.statement: Mandates the critical design rule that the bridge experiment use a parallel representation family (independently generated representations Ra=Ta(D), Rb=Tb(D), neither a deterministic function of the other) rather than only a deterministic sequential chain, since a sequential chain's data-processing constraint H(Q|Rn)<=H(Q|R(n-1)) structurally prevents testing non-monotone adequacy -- directly addressing the H-C category error found in the prior KR-REP-REDUCTION reviews.

rows.anchor: The mathematical carrier must be the minimum structure required by the actual experiment. Do not declare: set, graph, hypergraph, lattice, matroid, closure system, rewriting system, category, algebra as the carrier before the experiment. ... clearly distinguish: experimental carrier, mathematical ca
rows.statement: Prohibits declaring any specific mathematical carrier (set, graph, hypergraph, lattice, matroid, closure system, rewriting system, category, algebra) before the experiment runs, requiring the carrier to be the minimum structure the experiment actually needs, and mandates keeping experimental carrier, mathematical carrier, and future KnowledgeOS knowledge representation explicitly distinct with no unevidenced transfer between them.

rows.anchor: Use a finite structured source D ... rich enough to permit: redundancy, relational dependence, context dependence, individually removable elements, jointly non-removable groups, preservation and information-loss cases. ... For every source case store D, Q(D), contract parameters, transformation para
rows.statement: Requires the source data D to be a finite, deterministically-seeded structured source rich enough to permit redundancy, relational dependence, context dependence, individually removable elements, jointly non-removable groups, and both preservation and information-loss cases, with complete persistence of every source case's D, Q(D), contract parameters, transformation parameters, Zero ground truth, every representation, adequacy result, and decoder result, so no result depends on regenerated or hidden data.

rows.anchor: At minimum construct representations with: R_A: information-preserving transformation, R_B: controlled lossy transformation, R_C: redundancy-removing transformation, R_D: relational/context-sensitive transformation. ... Do not optimize transformations after seeing results.
rows.statement: Requires at minimum four independently constructed representations -- R_A (information-preserving), R_B (controlled lossy), R_C (redundancy-removing), R_D (relational/context-sensitive) -- each fully specified (transformation ID, mathematical definition, input/output type, deterministic/random status, seed, provenance, expected information effect, contract dependencies) before results are examined, with no post-hoc optimization of transformations.

rows.anchor: Define Q BEFORE generating representations. ... Adequate(R) iff Q is recoverable from R. Operationally measure both empirical conditional information Hhat(Q|R) and exact semantic violation count Nviol ... Do not treat Hhat(Q|R)=0 as proof that population H(Q|R)=0.
rows.statement: Requires the preservation target Q to be defined before representations are generated, with adequacy defined as Q being recoverable from R, measured operationally via both empirical conditional information Hhat(Q|R) and an exact semantic violation count Nviol, while never treating the empirical Hhat(Q|R)=0 as proof of the population-level H(Q|R)=0.

rows.anchor: Use the existing Transformation-relative Zero definition. For elimination E_S: Zero(T,Pi,S;D) iff Pi(T(D)) = Pi(T(E_S(D))). ... NEVER DEFINE ZERO USING Q. Do NOT define: Zero(S) := Q(D) = Q(E_S(D)). That would build the desired bridge into the definition. Zero must use its own declared observable/op
rows.statement: Reuses the existing Transformation-relative Zero definition Zero(T,Pi,S;D) iff Pi(T(D))=Pi(T(E_S(D))), calculated independently from the preservation measurement, and issues a critical prohibition against ever defining Zero in terms of Q (e.g. Zero(S):=Q(D)=Q(E_S(D))), since that would build the desired bridge directly into the definition and make the experiment circular; Zero must use its own declared observable Pi while preservation uses Q.

rows.anchor: The experiment must deliberately seek all four cells: Zero+Adequate, Zero+Inadequate, Non-Zero+Adequate, Non-Zero+Inadequate. ... Zero+Inadequate would directly demonstrate that Zero is not sufficient for preservation. Non-Zero+Adequate would demonstrate that Zero is not necessary for preservation.
rows.statement: Requires a four-cell crossing design (Zero+Adequate, Zero+Inadequate, Non-Zero+Adequate, Non-Zero+Inadequate) deliberately populated in all cells where possible, noting that a populated Zero+Inadequate cell would show Zero is not sufficient for preservation and a populated Non-Zero+Adequate cell would show Zero is not necessary for it, while an empty cell must be investigated for generator/contract/transformation/sample-size/mathematical-necessity/implementation causes rather than treated as a law.

rows.anchor: Sweep the parameters that plausibly influence the relationship, including redundancy level, group size, representation loss, transformation class, observable Pi, preservation target Q, contract parameters, context dependence, relational interaction, source cardinality. Every parameter sweep must be
rows.statement: Requires declared-in-advance parameter sweeps across ten plausibly influential parameters (redundancy level, group size, representation loss, transformation class, observable Pi, preservation target Q, contract parameters, context dependence, relational interaction, source cardinality), explicitly forbidding silent tuning to obtain balanced four-way cells.

rows.anchor: At minimum stratify results by: transformation T, observable Pi, contract C, representation family, source structure, elimination size |S|. Report both pooled relationship and stratified relationship. An association that disappears after stratification must NOT be reported as a general Zero-preserva
rows.statement: Mandates confounding analysis stratifying results by transformation T, observable Pi, contract C, representation family, source structure, and elimination size |S|, reporting both pooled and stratified relationships, and forbidding reporting an association as a general Zero-preservation relationship if it disappears after stratification.

rows.anchor: Explicitly test T x Pi ... Do not classify transformations as simply relational / element-wise and stop there. Measure the actual interaction between transformation and observable. If higher-order or preservation behavior occurs under an element-wise transformation, record it. Do not resurrect the w
rows.statement: Requires explicitly testing the transformation-times-observable interaction (T x Pi) rather than stopping at a coarse relational/element-wise classification, recording higher-order or preservation behavior even under element-wise transformations, and explicitly forbidding resurrection of the already-withdrawn claim that relational transformations produce higher order while element-wise ones do not.

rows.anchor: retain the KR-ZERO determination-order analysis. Measure k=1,2,3,...,irreducible where feasible. Do not assume higher k -> more reduction, higher k -> less preservation, irreducibility -> information loss. Those are hypotheses to test, not definitions. In particular, do not equate determination orde
rows.statement: Requires retaining the KR-ZERO determination-order analysis (k=1,2,3,...,irreducible) in the bridge experiment while explicitly forbidding the assumptions that higher k implies more reduction, less preservation, or that irreducibility implies information loss -- these remain hypotheses to test -- and forbidding equating determination order with preservation boundary.

rows.anchor: Retain the KR-REP-REDUCTION principle that reduction is multidimensional. Measure independently ... encoded size, cardinality, field count, representation entropy, number of relations, number of records, other declared structural measures. Do NOT invent a single 'reduction score' ... If a decoder is
rows.statement: Requires measuring reduction multidimensionally (encoded size, cardinality, field count, entropy, relation count, record count, other declared measures) without inventing a single reduction score or assuming statistical independence among dimensions, and requires keeping representation adequacy strictly separate from decoder realization when a decoder is used, including an invertible recoding control to rule out decoder-sensitivity confounds.

rows.anchor: CONTROL A: A known information-preserving representation. CONTROL B: A known information-destroying representation. CONTROL C: An invertible recoding of the same representation. CONTROL D: A representation where Zero is known to vary independently of the preservation target ... CONTROL E: Positive c
rows.statement: Specifies six mandatory controls that must execute before any interpretation: A) a known information-preserving representation; B) a known information-destroying representation; C) an invertible recoding of the same representation; D) a representation where Zero is known to vary independently of the preservation target (if the generator permits); E) a positive control that the preservation test can detect information loss; F) a positive control that the Zero test can detect elimination differences.

rows.anchor: Use independent TRAIN and TEST populations. Declare seeds, population size, generator, parameter distributions before execution. Persist the complete populations. No training result may influence test generation. No test result may influence transformation definitions. No post-hoc filtering may be u
rows.statement: Requires independent train/test populations with pre-declared seeds, population size, generator, and parameter distributions, complete population persistence, and strict separation preventing training results from influencing test generation, test results from influencing transformation definitions, or post-hoc filtering to manufacture desired four-way cell counts.

rows.anchor: Q1: Can Zero occur while preservation fails? Q2: Can preservation hold while Zero fails? Q3: Does the Zero/Adequacy relationship survive changes in T? ... Q7: Does determination order predict preservation independently of T/Pi/C? Q8: Does the relationship survive an invertible recoding? Q9/Q10: Is a
rows.statement: Mandates that the implementation explicitly answer ten falsification questions (Q1-Q10) covering whether Zero can occur without preservation and vice versa, whether the relationship survives changes in T, Pi, contract, redundancy, an invertible recoding, whether determination order predicts preservation independent of T/Pi/C, and whether any apparent relationship is explained by transformation class or by the preservation target Q itself.

sources.note: Adversarial experiment protocol testing whether a Hilbert-space formalization (vector=K_t, inner product=semantic similarity, projection=Zero Lens, amplitude=probability, participation ratio=N_eff) survives KnowledgeOS's existing definitions, frozen results (FR-001), and adversarial cases; explicit anti-circularity, ablation, and representation-invariance requirements.

rows.anchor: DO NOT ASK HILBERT SPACE TO EXPLAIN KNOWLEDGEOS. ASK HILBERT SPACE TO SURVIVE KNOWLEDGEOS. The Hilbert-space proposal must survive: existing KnowledgeOS definitions, existing experiments, frozen negative results, adversarial cases, representation changes, statistical validation, mathematical consistency checks.
rows.statement: States the governing methodological principle for KR-HILBERT: do not ask Hilbert space to explain KnowledgeOS, ask it to survive KnowledgeOS -- the proposal must survive existing definitions, experiments, frozen negative results (notably FR-001), adversarial cases, representation changes, and statistical/mathematical consistency checks.

rows.anchor: H1: A KnowledgeOS epistemic state K_t can be represented as a vector in a Hilbert space without losing required epistemic distinctions. ... H9: The representation is invariant under admissible changes of basis... H12: The Hilbert model provides genuine explanatory or computational reduction rather than merely renaming existing structures.
rows.statement: States the full twelve-hypothesis test matrix (H1-H12): state-vector embedding without distinction loss; inner-product as semantic similarity; orthogonality as epistemic independence; Zero Lens as boundary-subspace projection; spectral decomposition as epistemic decomposition; amplitude as probability without collapsing into truth/knowledge; participation-ratio N_eff for effective complexity; Hilbert distance as semantic equivalence; representation invariance; revision/contradiction/supersession without corruption; coexistence with the E_t/K_t distinction; and genuine explanatory reduction versus mere renaming.

rows.anchor: Do NOT equate mathematical constructs merely because they have similar names. In particular, explicitly distinguish: geometric orthogonality / probabilistic independence, vector similarity / semantic similarity, norm / confidence, amplitude / probability, projection / epistemic boundary, spectral decomposition / epistemic decomposition, distance / semantic equivalence, participation ratio / effective hypothesis complexity.
rows.statement: Mandates explicitly distinguishing eight pairs of mathematically-named-alike but conceptually distinct constructs (geometric orthogonality vs probabilistic independence, vector similarity vs semantic similarity, norm vs confidence, amplitude vs probability, projection vs epistemic boundary, spectral decomposition vs epistemic decomposition, distance vs semantic equivalence, participation ratio vs effective hypothesis complexity) -- a mapping is accepted only if the required properties are demonstrated, not merely intuitively appealing.

rows.anchor: phi_K : KnowledgeState -> H, phi_E : Evidence -> H_E, and, where needed: phi_H : Hypothesis -> H_H. Do not assume these spaces are identical. Investigate whether they can legitimately be identified.
rows.statement: Specifies the formal starting model: separate embedding maps phi_K:KnowledgeState->H, phi_E:Evidence->H_E, phi_H:Hypothesis->H_H into a generic (not assumed finite-dimensional, separable, or canonically based) inner-product space, with identity between the spaces to be investigated, not assumed.

rows.anchor: Construct two epistemic states with identical represented vector but different knowledge attribution. Construct two vectors that are geometrically close but epistemically different. Determine whether the Hilbert representation itself can preserve the distinction. If not, record: [NEG] Hilbert representation collapses E_t/K_t distinction.
rows.statement: Mandates Experiment B (E_t vs K_t) as testing whether two epistemic states with an identical Hilbert vector can have different knowledge attribution, and whether geometrically close vectors can be epistemically different -- recording [NEG] if the Hilbert representation collapses the E_t/K_t distinction.

rows.anchor: Do NOT define semantic similarity using the inner product itself. There must be an independent reference criterion. Otherwise the experiment is circular. ... A test is INVALID if the reference criterion is defined using the proposed Hilbert representation. ... Whenever a proposed result is definitional rather than empirical, label it: [DEF] and do not count it as experimental confirmation.
rows.statement: States the anti-circularity rule: no test may define its reference criterion using the Hilbert construct under test (e.g. 'Hilbert similarity works because semantic similarity is defined as Hilbert similarity' is invalid); results that are definitional rather than empirical must be labeled [DEF] and not counted as experimental confirmation.

rows.anchor: K1 ≡sem K2 iff ||K1-K2|| < epsilon must be tested. This is NOT automatically an equivalence relation. Test: reflexivity, symmetry, transitivity. Construct explicit counterexamples if transitivity fails. Also test representation invariance: basis rotation, orthogonal transformation, unitary transformation, scaling, coordinate transformation, alternative embeddings.
rows.statement: Mandates Experiment D testing whether the proposed epsilon-ball semantic-equivalence definition (||K1-K2||<epsilon) is actually reflexive, symmetric, and transitive (constructing counterexamples if not), and whether it is invariant under basis rotation/orthogonal/unitary transformations, scaling, coordinate change, and alternative embeddings.

rows.anchor: This experiment MUST respect FR-001. Construct hypothesis families with: identical pairwise similarity distributions, different higher-order dependence... Ask: Can Hilbert pairwise geometry distinguish the families? If not: [NEG] pairwise Hilbert geometry cannot solve family-level complexity. Then test whether a richer Hilbert construction such as: tensor structure, density operators, covariance operators, Gram matrices, higher-order operators can preserve the required family-level structure.
rows.statement: Mandates Experiment M explicitly respecting the FROZEN FR-001 boundary: constructs hypothesis families with identical pairwise similarity distributions but different higher-order dependence/grouping/joint structure, testing whether Hilbert pairwise geometry can distinguish them (predicting [NEG] per FR-001), then testing whether richer constructions (tensor structure, density operators, covariance operators, Gram matrices, higher-order operators) can preserve family-level structure -- with no automatic promotion of any richer construction.

rows.anchor: Treat Linga/Yoni strictly as interpretive research lenses. ... Do NOT test metaphysical truth. Test only structural correspondence. ... Do not conclude: Linga = Hilbert space or: Yoni = Hilbert space unless an explicit structure-preserving correspondence is demonstrated.
rows.statement: Mandates Experiment N treating Linga/Yoni strictly as interpretive research lenses when testing whether the Hilbert model provides a useful mathematical realization of the metaphor, explicitly forbidding concluding Linga=Hilbert-space or Yoni=Hilbert-space absent a demonstrated structure-preserving correspondence.

rows.anchor: Kernel inclusion requires: 1. necessity 2. irreducibility 3. semantic stability 4. representation invariance 5. preservation of existing invariants 6. evidence across multiple scenarios. ... If an operation is derivable from existing primitives, classify: [INF] or [EXP] derivable capability not kernel primitive.
rows.statement: States a six-criterion kernel-inclusion test (necessity, irreducibility, semantic stability, representation invariance, preservation of existing invariants, evidence across multiple scenarios) for evaluating whether any Hilbert operation (projection, inner product, decomposition, state update, similarity, probability, selection) is genuinely irreducible, versus classifiable as a derivable capability.

rows.anchor: For every successful Hilbert correspondence, perform ablation. Remove: A. Hilbert geometry B. embedding C. inner product D. projection E. probabilistic interpretation F. basis structure ... A result that can be obtained equally well without Hilbert structure is not evidence that Hilbert space is foundational.
rows.statement: Mandates an ablation requirement: for every successful Hilbert correspondence, remove each of six structural components (geometry, embedding, inner product, projection, probabilistic interpretation, basis structure) to determine whether the claimed capability genuinely depends on Hilbert structure -- a result obtainable equally well without it is not evidence Hilbert space is foundational.

rows.anchor: Construct adversarial cases specifically designed to break the mapping. At minimum include: 1. geometrically close but semantically different ... 13. family-level dependence invisible pairwise ... 16. two vectors with same norm but different epistemic status. Do not protect the model from these cases.
rows.statement: Mandates sixteen specific adversarial test cases designed to break the Hilbert mapping (geometrically-close-but-semantically-different, geometrically-distant-but-equivalent, orthogonal-but-dependent, correlated-but-orthogonal, unknown!=absent, contradiction!=unknown, equal-posterior multiple hypotheses, high-probability-false/low-probability-true hypotheses, same-channel validation failure, basis-change instability, epsilon-transitivity failure, family-level dependence invisible pairwise, revision-with-historical-identity, same-vector-different-provenance, same-norm-different-epistemic-status), explicitly forbidding protecting the model from them.

rows.anchor: MATHEMATICAL: proven from definitions/axioms. EMPIRICAL: supported by simulation/data. CONCEPTUAL: useful structural analogy or interpretation. Never use one as evidence for another. ... Do not use 'PROVEN' unless an actual mathematical proof has been supplied.
rows.statement: Mandates keeping three result types strictly separate (Mathematical/proven-from-axioms, Empirical/simulation-supported, Conceptual/structural-analogy) and never using one as evidence for another, reserving the word 'PROVEN' only for an actual supplied mathematical proof.

rows.anchor: The experiment is successful even if Hilbert space is refuted. Success means: We learn exactly which mappings work, which mappings fail, which require additional assumptions, and which remain unresolved. A negative result is a successful research result. experiment.assumptions: epsilon-ball proximity is the proposed equivalence test
experiment.method: test reflexivity, symmetry, and transitivity of the epsilon-ball relation across the chain

rows.anchor: Witness: X~Uniform{-1,0,1}, Y=1[X=0]. Cov(X,Y)=0 → orthogonal. P(Y=1|X=0)=1 ≠ P(Y=1)=1/3 → NOT independent. Y is a deterministic function of X, and they are orthogonal. Orthogonality is a second-moment property; independence is a property of the whole joint distribution. They coincide only in the jointly-Gaussian case.
rows.statement: [NEG] H3 REFUTED as stated: constructs X~Uniform{-1,0,1} and Y=indicator(X=0), showing Cov(X,Y)=0 (orthogonal) while Y is a deterministic function of X (P(Y=1|X=0)=1 vs marginal P(Y=1)=1/3, clearly not independent) -- orthogonality is a second-moment property while independence concerns the whole joint distribution, coinciding only under an explicit (not free) jointly-Gaussian modeling assumption; verdict: refuted as stated, conditionally valid only under Gaussian restriction.

experiment.hypothesis: H3: orthogonality in the Hilbert representation legitimately represents epistemic independence
experiment.setup: X uniform on {-1,0,1}, Y=indicator(X=0)
experiment.assumptions: Cov as the second-moment orthogonality measure
experiment.method: compute Cov(X,Y) and compare conditional vs marginal probabilities of Y
experiment.result: Cov(X,Y)=0 (orthogonal) but Y is a deterministic function of X (clearly dependent)
experiment.interpretation: orthogonality and independence coincide only under joint Gaussianity, an explicit modeling commitment, not automatic
experiment.conclusion: [NEG] refuted as stated; conditionally valid under Gaussian assumption

rows.statement: Reconstructs the operation set as a typed family of 4 categorically distinct kinds of arrows (state transformations, assessments, historical reconstruction, governance predicates) rather than one homogeneous algebra of K x X -> K operations -- a substantially stronger and more disciplined result than forcing every operation into one signature shape.

rows.anchor: T2 o T1 in T_G iff the composed transformation satisfies the governance constraints. But even that needs a formal definition of G. ... Governance closure = structurally described, computationally unresolved.
rows.statement: States the correct (conditional, not universal) closure criterion for composed transformations under governance: T2 o T1 is in T_G if and only if the composed transformation itself satisfies the governance constraints -- but notes this criterion cannot yet be evaluated since G's algorithm, though well-typed (G(T,K,C,A,P) in {0,1}), is absent; governance closure is structurally described but computationally unresolved.

rows.anchor: We should now reject the simplistic architecture: T = one closed algebra of state transformations. ... KnowledgeOS transformation system containing: state transitions, assessments, governance predicates, historical reconstruction, possibly decisions/events, with typed connections between them. Wheth
rows.statement: States the step's central architectural conclusion, rejecting the simplistic 'one closed algebra' hypothesis in favor of a typed KnowledgeOS transformation system (state transitions, assessments, governance predicates, historical reconstruction, possibly decisions/events, all typed-connected), while explicitly leaving open whether this deserves the mathematical name category, partial algebra, transition system, or something else, per the governing mandate's instruction not to prematurely choose a structure.

rows.anchor: State represents domain knowledge. Assessment represents an evaluation of knowledge. Decision potentially represents a governed choice. Transformation changes domain state. Governance determines whether the transformation is admissible. History preserves/reconstructs evolution. These should therefor
rows.statement: Maps the mathematical typed-arrow separation directly onto a DDD boundary test: State, Assessment, Decision, Transformation, Governance and History are 6 distinct domain roles that should not automatically collapse into a single Aggregate, entity, or service, citing the corpus's own warning against conflating bounded contexts, aggregates, database tables and domain events.

rows.anchor: The hypothesis that KnowledgeOS has one closed transformation algebra over K is now weakened. ... KnowledgeOS has a typed transformation/assessment/governance system. ... The correct mathematical structure remains UNRESOLVED until equality, domains, composition and closure are fully specified.
rows.statement: Concludes Step 249 by weakening the one-closed-algebra hypothesis to a typed transformation/assessment/governance system, explicitly leaving the correct final mathematical structure UNRESOLVED pending full specification of equality, domains, composition and closure -- and sets Step 250 (Knowledge-State Equality and Identity Gate) as the next mandatory test, since undefined equality is identified as blocking Merge, Supersede and Replay specifically.

lineage_claims.quote: Step 250 -- Knowledge-State Equality and Identity Gate ... the current transformation system cannot be completed until that dependency is resolved.

rows.anchor: Validate: K x X -> Assessment. ... validation may subsequently trigger a state transition. Therefore Validate not-in T_K ... Instead Validate in A where A = {K x X -> Assessment}. This is one of the strongest findings in Step 250.
rows.statement: Reaffirms Validate as the strongest-evidenced operation, explicitly excluded from the state-transformation family T_K and placed instead in the assessment family A={K x X -> Assessment} -- reiterated as one of the step's strongest findings, consistent with S1613's identical conclusion.

rows.anchor: Revise = partial state transition with historical consequence is the strongest current characterization. ... signature refinement still OPEN [Revise: K x X x X' -harpoonup-> K x HistoryRelation, unpromoted since HistoryRelation is untyped].
rows.statement: Reaffirms Revise's characterization from Step 249: corpus-established as a partial state-changing operation with a historical consequence, but its exact richer signature (producing a typed HistoryRelation alongside the new state) remains open since HistoryRelation itself is untyped.

rows.anchor: The corpus defines Remove_x: K -harpoonup-> K. The operation is explicitly partial because removing one item may invalidate dependent knowledge. This means Remove in T_K is currently defensible. And Remove is partial. This is a stronger result than we had at Step 249.
rows.statement: Reclassifies Remove as CORPUS-ESTABLISHES (a partial operation Remove_x:K-harpoonup->K, since removing one item may invalidate dependent knowledge) -- the file explicitly calls this 'a stronger result than we had at Step 249', where the same operation was instead rated UNDEFINED at signature level (S1613); the two adjacent same-day step files disagree on Remove's status without either citing the other's specific verdict.

Supersede: at minimum, supersession requires identifying what is being superseded. That immediately creates an equality/identity dependency ... Supersede = UNRESOLVED with blocker
rows.statement: Reaffirms Add as a corpus-established partial operation (constrained by Invariant(K')=True), and reaffirms Supersede as UNRESOLVED, naming its blockers precisely as Equality, Identity, and TemporalSemantics -- consistent with and sharpening S1613's identification of equality as Supersede's blocker.

rows.statement: Assembles the strongest current typed-family structure S=(K,T,A,Q,E,H,D,G) with 8 named components (knowledge states, partial state transformations, assessments, queries, events, history, decisions, governance predicates) -- explicitly not the final structure, but the smallest currently defensible typed candidate family, extending S1613's 4-arrow-kind classification with Queries and Decisions made explicit.

rows.anchor: We can now establish four different kinds of arrows [epistemic production, assessment, decision, state transition] and: 5. Historical reconstruction (H -> K). ... the earlier notation T: K -> K is too narrow to describe the complete KnowledgeOS process. But T: K -> K may still correctly describe one
rows.statement: Names 5 categorically distinct arrow kinds (epistemic production: Observation/Evidence->Assertion; assessment: K->Assessment; decision: Assessment+Policy+Authority->Decision; state transition: K->K'; historical reconstruction: H->K), concluding the simple notation T:K->K is too narrow to describe the complete KnowledgeOS process even though it correctly describes one subfamily within it.

rows.anchor: Total algebra? NO. Universal state-transition algebra? NO, too broad. Partial state-transition family? YES -- strong candidate. Typed family? YES -- strongest current candidate, because Validate has a different codomain from Transform. Category? NOT YET. Monoid/semigroup? NOT ESTABLISHED.
rows.statement: Gives an explicit mathematical-classification verdict for the transformation system: not a total algebra, not a universal state-transition algebra (too broad), but confirmed as a partial state-transition family (supported by Add/Remove partiality) and, most strongly, a typed family (since Validate's Assessment codomain differs from Transform's K codomain) -- while explicitly declining category or monoid/semigroup status as not yet demonstrated.

rows.anchor: The candidate kernel cannot yet contain merely (K,T). It must at least distinguish State from Transition from Assessment from Decision from Event and History/Lineage. Whether these are all primitives of one final mathematical object is still open. ... Transition System = typed family of related tran
rows.statement: States the step's final conclusion and the most important kernel-design consequence: the candidate kernel must distinguish at least 6 roles (State, Transition, Assessment, Decision, Event, History/Lineage) rather than collapsing to (K,T); the strongest current hypothesis is that the Transition System is a typed family of related structures, not one closed algebra, though final mathematical closure remains unproven -- directly aligning with the parallel verifier track's typed-family conclusion (S1603, S1612).

lineage_claims.quote: Step 252 should construct: Canonical Vocabulary / Polysemy Audit ... we cannot finalize K, T, or equality while their component vocabulary is itself polysemous.

rows.anchor: inference is best treated as a process/mechanism, while determination is a recorded epistemic result. ... Validation is an operation/mechanism. Assessment is its possible output. Validation != Assessment. ... Validation should probably be a domain operation/process, not an entity called Validation.
rows.statement: Confirms and DDD-classifies two operation/output pairs: Inference (process, Input->Candidate) is distinct from Determination (recorded result, Assessment->EpistemicStanding); Validation (operation) is distinct from Assessment (its output), matching the earlier transition audit's Validate:KxX->Assessment finding and recommending Validation be modeled as a domain operation, not an entity.

rows.anchor: Op | Signature | Properties [11-operation algebra table: Add total idempotent commutative associative monotone; Remove total cascading not monotone NO TOTAL INVERSE; Merge join-semilattice; Split lossy on R; Supersede idempotent preserves the superseded assertion; Contradict symmetric irreflexive NO
rows.statement: Produces a fully executed 11-operation algebra table with formal signatures and properties (Add: total/idempotent/commutative/associative/monotone; Remove: total/cascading/not-monotone/no-total-inverse; Merge: join-semilattice; Split: lossy on R; Supersede: idempotent, preserves the superseded assertion per 218.21; Contradict: symmetric/irreflexive/not-transitive; Validate: total/deterministic/pure; Replay: deterministic/order-dependent; Transform: partial/deterministic/closed; Query: pure/monotone/temporally-correct; Compare: the equivalence relation), with 5 named refuted properties each backed by an executed counterexample.

rows.anchor: a3 was constructed to supersede a1. The contradiction predicate flagged it as a contradiction. Both assertions were open-ended, so their validity intervals genuinely overlap. Supersession and contradiction are indistinguishable to a pairwise predicate. ... (a') exclude interval-end from the id hash:
rows.statement: Reports the one failing probe (probe 6 of 14) as genuine unresolved theory, not a test defect: an assertion constructed to supersede another is also flagged as contradicting it, since supersession and contradiction are indistinguishable to a purely pairwise predicate when both assertions are open-ended and their intervals overlap; of three attempted repairs, one (closing the superseded interval) is refuted (breaks content-addressed identity and Valid), while two are viable -- (a') excluding interval-end from the identity hash (at the cost of making temporal validity mutable state) and (c) making Contradict discount differences already explained by the relation set R (no mutation needed) -- with implementation evidence (ReplayAssertion's immutability invariant) favoring (c), which independently re-derives, from the opposite direction, that R is not reducible to the assertion set A alone.

experiment.hypothesis: Contradict and Supersede are cleanly distinguishable predicates over pairs of assertions.
experiment.setup: construct a3 to supersede a1, both with open-ended validity intervals.
experiment.assumptions: pairwise evaluation of Contradict without reference to R
experiment.method: execute the contradiction predicate against the pair
experiment.result: a3 is flagged as contradicting a1 despite being intended as a supersession
experiment.interpretation: supersession and contradiction are indistinguishable to a pairwise-only predicate
experiment.limitations: single constructed example
experiment.conclusion: Contradict must be redefined to consult R (option c), or identity must exclude the interval end (option a'), each with distinct tradeoffs

rows.statement: Requires deriving the minimal necessary transformation signature (candidate range from T(K,o) to T(K,o,actor,authority,policy,evidence,context,time)) by testing 8 properties (determinism, closure, composability, identity operation, failure/rejection, replay, provenance, governance) rather than choosing a signature by syntactic convenience.

rows.statement: States the step's final synthesis formula (KnowledgeOS Kernel = Minimal Sufficient State Abstraction + Typed Transformation Semantics) with an explicit required ordering (congruence must be established before minimality; a complete operation registry must exist before any final K), and sets Step 256 as the Formal Operation Signature Registry -- a full per-operation schema (Name/Domain/Codomain/Preconditions/Postconditions/Required State Information/Provenance Dependence/Policy Dependence/History Dependence/Determinism/Computability) needed before the congruence test can be systematically executed against every mandatory operation.

lineage_claims.quote: Step 256 -- Formal Operation Signature Registry ... Step 256 should therefore formalize the complete operation/signature registry before any further kernel reduction.

rows.anchor: we should not assume closure: T_i,T_j in T => T_j o T_i in T. The earlier audit already found that the governed transformation subset is not demonstrated closed under composition.
rows.statement: Reaffirms the corpus's established finding that the governed transformation subset is not closed under composition, applying it to the operation-registry construction: composition T_j o T_i is only meaningful when Codomain(T_i) intersects Domain(T_j), and closure must never be assumed.

rows.anchor: T_Add: K x X -> K, T_Merge: K x X x X -> K, Validate: K x E -> Result, Approve: Candidate x Authority -> ApprovedCandidate. Therefore KnowledgeOS may be better modeled as a typed transition system than as a single algebra.
rows.statement: Confirms operations need not share one homogeneous signature shape by giving 4 explicitly differently-typed example operations, reaffirming the typed-transition-system (not single algebra) conclusion already reached in Steps 249-250.

rows.anchor: Validate not-equiv Transform. This prevents a common category error in the kernel. ... Command is not Transformation ... Command -> Decision -> Transformation -> NewState ... Event != T. The corpus already distinguishes Command -> Transformation -> Event.
rows.statement: Reaffirms three category-error-preventing non-collapses for the operation vocabulary: Validate != Transform (validation may determine valid/invalid without changing K); Command != Transformation (command is intent/request, not the state change itself); Event != Transformation (an event records an occurrence, distinct from the state-evolution-defining function).

rows.anchor: transformation: K x Op x Policy x Authority -> K [changes K: YES, appends History: YES]. assessment: P x Evidence x Context x Policy -> Sigma [changes K: no, appends History: no]. decision: Assessment x Authority -> Determination [changes K: no until asserted, appends History: YES]. governance actio
rows.statement: Classifies all acts into 4 kinds by a precise signature/effect table (transformation: mutates K, appends history; assessment: neither; decision: appends history without mutating K until subsequently asserted; governance action: appends history without mutating K), concluding validate and assess are the ONLY two operations that never change K -- they are queries wearing operation names, so any implementation where validation mutates state has conflated assessment with transformation, exactly the error Step 232.4 warns against.

rows.anchor: The four operations do not require identical semantic inputs. Therefore a single universal signature T:KxP->K is likely too coarse. Instead T = {T1,...,Tn} should be treated as a typed family. ... Operation dependency != State membership. Transform(K,Policy) does not imply Policy subseteq K. Similar
rows.statement: Confirms via the 4-operation dependency comparison that a single universal transformation signature is too coarse (the operations need different inputs), reinforcing the typed-family conclusion, and restates the operation-dependency != state-membership principle with concrete Transform/Policy and Merge/Evidence examples.

lexical.anchor: T1,T2 in T_G does not necessarily imply T2 o T1 in T_G. The audit correctly identifies this as a closure failure. Therefore we must distinguish T from T_G. ... 'transformation algebra' = working name, not established mathematical classification.

rationale_evidence.statement: Establishes the architectural separation between a transformation's effect T(K) and its permissibility Allowed(T,K,C,A,P,E), proposing a pipeline (K,T,C,A,P,E) -> Admissible? -> K'=T(K,theta), grounded in the corpus's own separation of transition from permission to transition.

rationale_evidence.anchor: 10 operations classified: Transform (State transition, CORPUS ESTABLISHES); Validate (Assessment, CORPUS ESTABLISHES); Add (Partial state operation, CORPUS ESTABLISHES); Revise (PARTIALLY VERIFIED); Merge/Supersede/Split/Remove/Reject/Replay (OPEN).
rationale_evidence.statement: Classifies 10 mandate-required operations against the Step-232 audit: Transform, Validate and Add are corpus-established (with distinct roles: state transition, assessment, and explicitly partial operation respectively); Revise is only partially verified; Merge, Supersede, Split, Remove, Reject and Replay are all OPEN -- explicitly matching the detailed Step-232 audit rather than the earlier assumption that every operation belongs to one algebra.

rationale_evidence.anchor: Revise involves new state + historical relation. ... revision appears to involve two outputs: (K',r) where r in HistoryRelation. ... because the corpus does not explicitly type the historical relation, we must keep this PROPOSED rather than promoted.
rationale_evidence.statement: Proposes that Revise may actually produce two outputs -- the revised state K' and a historical relation r in HistoryRelation -- since the historical fact K leadsto K' is not necessarily part of K' itself, but keeps this candidate signature (K x X x X' -harpoonup-> K x HistoryRelation) explicitly PROPOSED, not promoted, since the corpus never types HistoryRelation.

rationale_evidence.anchor: To determine whether one state supersedes another, we need some notion of K1 = K2 or at least identity of the relevant knowledge object. Since knowledge-state equality remains undefined, the operation cannot yet be formally closed. Supersede = OPEN and the blocker is: Equality.
rationale_evidence.statement: Identifies undefined Knowledge-State equality as the specific and sole blocker preventing Supersede from being formally closed -- a precise, load-bearing dependency rather than a vague open item.

rationale_evidence.anchor: The key question is whether removing an object means: deleting it; marking it invalid; superseding it; retracting its epistemic status; removing it from a projection while preserving provenance. These are mathematically different operations. Remove = UNDEFINED at signature level. ... Reject listed b
rationale_evidence.statement: Records Remove as undefined even at the signature level, since 'removing' could mean 5 mathematically distinct operations (deletion, invalidity marking, supersession, epistemic-status retraction, or projection-removal preserving provenance); records Reject as effectively abandoned in the audited corpus (OPEN); and records Replay as equality-dependent, since whether replay must reproduce K_n exactly or merely observationally returns to the still-open equality question.

rationale_evidence.statement: Reaffirms Add as a corpus-established partial operation (constrained by Invariant(K')=True), and reaffirms Supersede as UNRESOLVED, naming its blockers precisely as Equality, Identity, and TemporalSemantics -- consistent with and sharpening S1613's identification of equality as Supersede's blocker.

sources.note: Resolves the corpus's long-standing 'eleven competing epistemic-status vocabularies' problem by classifying 24 discovered terms into 5 categories (3 irreducible states, 5 derived, 4 relations, 4 lifecycle, 7 governance, 1 collision); derives a minimal Sigma={Unknown,Supported,Refuted}, confirms Sigma-perp-Gamma orthogonality by 4 concrete quadrant examples, and relocates supersession/contestation to a relation R subseteq AxA -- explicitly retracting the verifier's own prior escalation of this question to the human author (S1605's B1) as malformed, closing it by derivation instead.

rows.anchor: I asked the author to choose among five status vocabularies. That question was malformed, and the refusal was correct. The 'eleven competing vocabularies' were never competing. They are FIVE DIFFERENT KINDS OF THING crammed into one field. Once separated, the epistemic core is uniquely determined at
rows.statement: Retracts the verifier's own prior escalation of the status-vocabulary question to the author (B1 in S1605): the framing of 'competing vocabularies' was itself malformed, since the 11+ terms are not alternatives for one dimension but instances of 5 different kinds of thing conflated into a single field; once separated, the true epistemic core is uniquely determined at 3 states.

lineage_claims.quote: B1 -- status vocabulary. Normative. AUTHOR INPUT REQUIRED.

rows.anchor: All discovered vocabularies (executed enumeration, 24 terms) [table with file counts and numbered-step spans, e.g. Unknown 45 files/steps 12..242, Supported 24/8..245, ...]
rows.statement: Executes a corpus-wide enumeration finding 24 distinct status-like terms in use (Unknown, Supported, Rejected, Inferred, Candidate, Observed, Accepted, Confirmed, Superseded, Conflicted, Approved, Validated, Refuted, Proposed, Contested, Established, Corroborated, Verified, Disputed, Determined, Authoritative, Deprecated, Retired, and their file/step-span counts) -- the empirical basis for the subsequent semantic classification.

rows.anchor: Test applied to every term: is it a property of ONE assertion, a relation between TWO, a lifecycle marker, a governance act, or derivable from the others? [5 categories: STATE n=3 Unknown/Supported/Refuted; DERIVED n=5; RELATION(binary) n=4; LIFECYCLE n=4; GOVERNANCE n=7; COLLISION n=1 Determined]
rows.statement: Classifies all 24 discovered terms via a 5-way decisive test (unary epistemic property vs binary relation vs lifecycle marker vs governance act vs derivable-from-others) into: 3 irreducible unary epistemic states (Unknown, Supported, Refuted), 5 derived values (Conflicted, Observed, Established, Inferred, Confirmed), 4 binary relations (Superseded, Contested, Corroborated, Disputed), 4 lifecycle markers (Proposed, Candidate, Deprecated, Retired), 7 governance acts (Approved, Rejected, Accepted, Validated, Verified, Authoritative, Invalidated), and 1 genuine terminological collision (Determined).

rows.anchor: Superseded is a RELATION, not a state. It requires two assertions. Step 218.21 states this itself: C1 --superseded--> C2, not delete(C1). ... Deprecated is explicitly NOT epistemic -- step-218.22 boxes Deprecated != Falsified. ... Observed and Inferred differ by EVIDENCE TYPE, not epistemic state. .
rows.statement: Gives the decisive individual justifications behind the classification, each grounded in corpus citation: Superseded requires two assertions (step-218.21's C1-->superseded-->C2, never a delete); Deprecated is explicitly non-epistemic per step-218.22 (Deprecated != Falsified); Observed and Inferred both mean Supported but differ only in evidence type (belongs in E, not Sigma); Established reduces to Supported plus an uncodified corroboration threshold with no distinguishing operation; Determined is a genuine terminological collision (a status at steps 186-189, an aggregate at step 196.26).

rows.anchor: I proposed a four-state set (Unknown/Supported/Refuted/Conflicted). That is one too many. Conflicted(A,K) := exists A' in K: same (subject,predicate), different object, overlapping validity, same context, neither Refuted. Conflicted is computable from the state. No operation requires it as a stored
rows.statement: Corrects a previously proposed 4-state Sigma set (adding Conflicted) down to a minimal 3-state Sigma={Unknown, Supported, Refuted}, by giving an explicit computable definition of Conflicted(A,K) as a derived predicate over the state (same subject/predicate, differing object, overlapping validity, same context, neither Refuted) that no operation requires as a stored primitive, and warning that storing it duplicates derivable information and risks an update anomaly (stored flag disagreeing with computed value).
invariants: Supported required by every other operation

rows.anchor: 4-state (adds Conflicted): REFUTED as minimal. 6-state historical (Proposed/Supported/Established/Superseded/Contested/Invalidated): REFUTED -- mixes four categories ... Only Supported is an epistemic state, and Contested is a relation. Two orthogonal dimensions: CONFIRMED. 3-state core + separate d
rows.statement: Tests and refutes two larger candidate status sets: a 4-state candidate (Conflicted refuted as derived, per the prior finding) and a 6-state 'historical' candidate (Proposed/Supported/Established/Superseded/Contested/Invalidated) which is shown to mix all 5 category types at once (lifecycle, epistemic, derived, relation, governance) with only Supported actually being an epistemic state; the surviving candidate is a 3-state epistemic core plus separate orthogonal dimensions.

rows.anchor: Sigma perp Gamma -- orthogonality CONFIRMED by construction. All four quadrants are meaningful and occur in the domain: [Supported/not-approved; Unknown/permitted; Refuted/still-authoritative; Supported/rejected]. Corpus support: step-194.19 boxes EpistemicStrength != GovernanceStatus; step-008 sepa
rows.statement: Confirms by explicit 2x2 construction that epistemic status (Sigma) and governance status (Gamma) are orthogonal dimensions: all four quadrant combinations (Supported+not-approved; Unknown+permitted; Refuted+still-authoritative; Supported+rejected) correspond to meaningful, realistic domain cases, and the corpus itself states the separation (step-194.19: EpistemicStrength != GovernanceStatus; step-008: acceptance vs commitment; step-232.4: Validation->Assessment) even though it then violates it by storing governance terms inside Sigma.
invariants: Sigma and Gamma are orthogonal: a single field cannot carry both without information loss

rows.statement: Derives the operational consequences of the 3-state Sigma resolution: the Assertion tuple becomes A=(id,P,Sigma,E,tau,Pi) with Sigma restricted to {Unknown,Supported,Refuted}; Gamma (governance) attaches separately to a governance context, not to A; Superseded becomes a relation in R or History rather than a Sigma value; the previously blocked state-consistency sub-predicate of Valid(K) (from S1603/S1605) becomes computable now that Sigma is fixed; Merge/Supersede become well-typed since supersession operates on the relation rather than mutating a status field.

rows.anchor: K_t shape: relations must live somewhere -- this constrains the container. UL: 24 terms reduce to 3 states + 4 relations + 7 governance + 4 lifecycle. The 'eleven vocabularies' dissolve.
rows.statement: Notes a downstream constraint on the still-open K_t shape blocker (B2): since relations (Superseded, Contested, Corroborated, Disputed) now need an explicit home in the container, this constrains what K_t's tuple/shape can be; and restates the overall UL resolution -- the notorious 'eleven competing vocabularies' dissolve into a clean 3+4+7+4 partition (states + relations + governance + lifecycle).

rows.anchor: Recommended canonical model: Sigma: Assertion -> {Unknown,Supported,Refuted} epistemic, minimal, DERIVED from Assessment.
